notes: a point KICKOFF of lane TEAM A becomes TEAM A-KICKOFF; the spans merge the same way

methods.name: Clear
methods.brief: Empties every lane of its points and spans, keeping the lanes and the bounds.

methods.name: Copy
methods.brief: Returns an independent set built from the same lane names and bounds, with their points, spans and blocks.
methods.returns: a stzTimeLines whose lanes hold what these lanes hold
notes: changing the copy, or the original afterwards, leaves the other as it was; use Content to read everything

classes.name: stzListParser
classes.brief: Walks through a list with a cursor, visiting the positions you choose: from a start to an end by a step, forward or backwards.
classes.description: A parser is built over a non-empty list with new stzListParser(aList) or StzListParserQ(aList); no stzList method builds one. Parse chooses the positions to visit (ParsedPositions) and ParsedItems answers the items there; the cursor, read with CurrentPosition and CurrentItem, moves with NextPosition, PreviousPosition and the Nth forms, which count visited positions, not list positions, so with a step of 2 NextNthPosition(2) advances four list positions. NextItem and PreviousItem move the cursor and answer the item, so two calls give two different items. Reset parses again with the default start, end and step (1, the last position, 1 until a SetDefault... call changes them), not with the last Parse. Positions count from 1. Moving past the last visited position, or before the first, raises a Ring error (R2, array access out of range) and leaves the cursor in place; Parse does not check the positions against the list, and ParsedItems raises when one is outside it. The base class stzParser only keeps a source value; a stzListParser does not fill it, so read the list with List.
classes.example:
o1.Parse(3, 8, 2)
? @@( o1.ParsedPositions() )
#--> [ 3, 5, 7 ]
? @@( o1.ParsedItems() )
#--> [ "c", "e", "g" ]
? o1.NextItem()
#--> e
? o1.CurrentPosition()
#--> 5
o1.Reset()
? o1.CurrentPosition()
#--> 1
o2 = new stzListParser([ "שלום", "مرحبا", "😀", "ok" ])
? o2.NextItem()
#--> مرحبا

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a parser over a non-empty list and parses it from the first position to the last, one step at a time.

parameters.name: paList
parameters.role: the list to walk through, which must not be empty, a text or an empty list raises an error

methods.returns: nothing; the object is built, with the cursor on position 1
notes: the parser keeps the list as given; stzParser.Source of a stzListParser answers an empty text, so read the list with List

methods.name: List
methods.brief: Returns the list being parsed.

methods.name: ParsedPositions
methods.brief: Returns the positions the current parse visits, in order.
methods.returns: a list of numbers, positions in the list counted from 1
notes: after Parse(3, 8, 2) on a list of 8 it is [ 3, 5, 7 ]

methods.name: StartPosition
methods.brief: Returns the position the current parse starts at.

methods.name: EndPosition
methods.brief: Returns the position the current parse was asked to stop at.
notes: after Parse(3, 8, 2) it is 8, though the last position visited is 7

methods.name: NumberOfSteps
methods.brief: Returns the step of the current parse: the distance between two visited positions.
notes: it is a step length, not a count of positions; use len(ParsedPositions()) for the count

methods.name: Parse
methods.brief: Chooses which positions to visit, from a start to an end by a step, and puts the cursor on the first one.

parameters.name: pnStart
parameters.role: the first position, a number or :First, also accepted as :From = n

parameters.name: pnEnd
parameters.role: the last position, a number or :Last, also accepted as :To = n

parameters.name: pnStep
parameters.role: the distance between two positions, a negative number walks backwards, also accepted as :Step = n

notes: Parse(5, 2, -1) on abcde visits 5, 4, 3, 2; no check is made against the list, so Parse(1, 20, 1) on a list of 5 gives 20 positions and ParsedItems then raises an error

methods.name: SetStartPosition
methods.brief: Changes the position the parse starts at and parses again, keeping the end and the step.

parameters.name: pnStart
parameters.role: the new first position

methods.returns: nothing; the parser is re-parsed and the cursor goes to the first position

methods.name: SetEndPosition
methods.brief: Changes the position the parse stops at and parses again, keeping the start and the step.

parameters.name: pnEnd
parameters.role: the new last position

methods.returns: nothing; the parser is re-parsed and the cursor goes to the first position

methods.name: SetNumberOfSteps
methods.brief: Changes the step of the parse and parses again, keeping the start and the end.

parameters.name: pnSteps
parameters.role: the new distance between two positions

methods.returns: nothing; the parser is re-parsed and the cursor goes to the first position

methods.name: SetCurrentPosition
methods.brief: Moves the cursor to a position that belongs to the parse, or back to the default one with :Default.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: the position to move to, a number in ParsedPositions, or :Default for the default current position

methods.returns: nothing; a position outside the parse, or any other value, is ignored without an error
notes: SetCurrentPosition(5) on a parse of 4, 6 leaves the cursor where it was

methods.name: CurrentPosition
methods.brief: Returns the position the cursor is on.

methods.name: ResetCurrentPosition
methods.brief: Puts the cursor back on the default current position when the parse contains it, otherwise on the first parsed position.

methods.name: NextNthPosition
methods.brief: Moves the cursor forward by n visited positions and returns the position it lands on.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: how many visited positions to advance, counted in the parse, not in the list

methods.returns: a number, the new cursor position
notes: with a step of 2, NextNthPosition(2) advances four list positions; NthNextPosition is the same call
warnings: moving past the last visited position raises an error (R2, array access out of range) instead of answering 0, and the cursor stays where it was; NextNthPosition(9) on 5 positions and NextPosition on the last one both raise

methods.name: NextPosition
methods.brief: Moves the cursor to the next visited position and returns it.
methods.returns: a number, the new cursor position
warnings: moving past the last visited position raises an error (R2, array access out of range) and leaves the cursor in place

methods.name: PreviousNthPosition
methods.brief: Moves the cursor back by n visited positions and returns the position it lands on.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: how many visited positions to go back, counted in the parse, not in the list

methods.returns: a number, the new cursor position
notes: NthPreviousPosition is the same call
warnings: moving before the first visited position raises an error (R2, array access out of range) instead of answering 0, and the cursor stays where it was

methods.name: PreviousPosition
methods.brief: Moves the cursor to the previous visited position and returns it.
methods.returns: a number, the new cursor position
warnings: moving before the first visited position raises an error (R2, array access out of range) and leaves the cursor in place

methods.name: ParsedItems
methods.brief: Returns the items at the visited positions, in the order visited.
notes: with positions beyond the list it raises an error (R2, array access out of range)

methods.name: CurrentItem
methods.brief: Returns the item under the cursor, without moving it.

methods.name: NextNthItem
methods.brief: Moves the cursor forward by n visited positions and returns the item it lands on.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: how many visited positions to advance

methods.returns: the item at the new position
notes: NthNextItem is the same call
warnings: moving past the last visited position raises an error, as NextNthPosition does

methods.name: NextItem
methods.brief: Moves the cursor to the next visited position and returns the item there.
methods.returns: the item at the new position
notes: the cursor moves, so two calls give two different items
warnings: moving past the last visited position raises an error (R2, array access out of range)

methods.name: PreviousNthItem
methods.brief: Moves the cursor back by n visited positions and returns the item it lands on.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: how many visited positions to go back

methods.returns: the item at the new position
notes: NthPreviousItem is the same call
warnings: moving before the first visited position raises an error, as PreviousNthPosition does

methods.name: PreviousItem
methods.brief: Moves the cursor to the previous visited position and returns the item there.
methods.returns: the item at the new position
warnings: moving before the first visited position raises an error (R2, array access out of range)

methods.name: Reset
methods.brief: Parses again with the default start, end and step, and puts the cursor back to its default.
notes: it returns to the defaults (1, :End, 1), not to the last Parse

classes.name: stzListPerformer
classes.brief: Applies an expression to the items of a list, to all of them or to some, either rewriting the list (Perform) or only reading the results (Yield).
classes.description: Build one with new stzListPerformer(aList) or over a stzList object; it keeps its own copy, so what you passed in is not changed, and Content gives the result of the Perform calls. The W forms (PerformW, YieldW) choose the items by a condition written the same way, and the On forms by positions. Inside an expression len() counts bytes, not letters. classes.name: stzListProvidedAsString
classes.brief: Holds a list that was provided as text, such as '[ 1, 2, "A" ]', and tells its values from its variable names.
classes.description: The idea, from the comment in its file: a list written as text can hold values (1, "A", [ 5, "V" ]) or variable names (n1, aList1), and a search must be able to look for a value wherever it is hosted or for a variable whatever its value. The text is read, never evaluated: nothing in it is run and no variable is looked up. What is read. The text must be one list in square brackets (spaces, tabs and new lines around it and between its items are free). It is cut at the commas that sit directly in that list, so a comma inside a quoted text, a nested list, a pair of parentheses or braces does not cut. A quote opened with ', " or ` ends at the next quote of the same kind, and a backslash is an ordinary character, as in Ring, which has no escapes. A single trailing comma is allowed, as in Ring. Any other text is NOT well formed (IsWellFormed): an unclosed bracket or quote, a mismatched closer, something after the closing bracket, an empty item such as [ 1,, 2 ]; it has no items and every test on it answers FALSE. Each item is of one kind: value      a number (-3, 2.5, 1e3, 0x1F), a quoted text, a :name, or a nested list (whose inside is not examined) variable   a bare name made of letters (accented, Hebrew or any other), digits and _, not starting with a digit, optionally starting with @ or $ and optionally dotted: n1, aList1, oObj1, @x, $g, oObj.name. TRUE, FALSE and NULL are names here, since the text is not evaluated other      anything else, such as 1+2, f(x), or :name = "v" written directly in the list The empty list [ ] holds no value and no variable name, so it is neither a list of values nor a list of variable names nor a mix: all three tests answer FALSE for it, as IsListOfNumbers does for an empty list. An item of kind other keeps a list from being only values or only variables, and does not prevent it from mixing both.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.Items() )
#--> [ "1", '"A"', '[ 5, "V" ]' ]
? o1.IsListOfValues()
#--> 1
o2 = new stzListProvidedAsString("[ n1, aList1 ]")
? o2.IsListOfVariables()
#--> 1

classes.name: stzListRandom
classes.brief: Draws positions and items at random from a list, and shuffles the whole list, a section of it or the runs of one kind of item.
classes.description: Built around a list or a stzList. The drawing methods (RandomPosition, RandomItem, NRandomItems and their Except forms) leave the list as it is. Randomize, Shuffle and the section and typed variants change it in place and answer nothing, while Randomized and the other names ending in Randomized answer a shuffled copy. The typed shuffles (numbers, strings, lists, objects) only reorder items of that kind that sit next to each other: [ 1, 2, 3, "a", 4, 5 ] can swap 1, 2 and 3 and swap 4 and 5, but a number never crosses the text. Two cautions: NRandomPositions(0) never returns, and RandomItemExceptPosition on a list of one item raises R2. The draws are random, so promises can only be made about shape and ranges.
classes.example:
? o1.NumberOfItems()
#--> 5
? o1.RandomPositionGreaterThan(5)
#--> 0
? len(o1.NRandomItems(3))
#--> 3
? sum(o1.Randomized())
#--> 150
? o1.Content()[1]
#--> 10

classes.name: stzListRemover
classes.brief: Deletes items from a list: every occurrence of an item, the nth or the first or the last, the item at a position, a section, or several positions at once.
classes.description: It is the removing helper of stzList, which builds one over itself for its RemoveW method; build one with new stzListRemover when you only need to delete. It works on its own copy, so a stzList passed in is never changed, and you read the result with Content. A verb (RemoveAll, RemoveFirstItem, RemoveSection ...) edits the held list in place and returns nothing, its Q form returning the remover for chaining; the past-tense forms (AllOccurrencesRemoved, NthItemRemoved, FirstItemRemoved, LastItemRemoved) return an edited copy and leave the remover alone. Positions count from 1. Items are matched whole and with case; the CS forms take 0 to ignore case. Three limits found today: a negative position given to RemoveItemAtPosition (and so to RemoveAt, RemoveAtPosition and RemoveNthItem) kills the Ring process, RemoveLastItem raises on an empty list, and a position listed twice in RemoveItemsAtPositions deletes two different items.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.AllOccurrencesRemoved("a") )
#--> [ "b", "c" ]
? @@( o1.NthItemRemoved(2) )
#--> [ "a", "a", "c", "a" ]
o1.RemoveNthOccurrence(2, "a")
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ "a", "b", "c", "a" ]
o1.RemoveSection(2, 3)
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ "a", "a" ]
o2 = new stzListRemover([ "שלום", "😀", "שלום", "x" ])
o2.RemoveAll("שלום")
? @@( o2.Content() )
#--> [ "😀", "x" ]

classes.name: stzListReplacer
classes.brief: Changes the items of a list in place: one item, every occurrence of a value, a section, or a chosen set of positions.
classes.description: Reach for it when you need to rewrite part of a list and keep the object: the methods act on the held list and return nothing, so read the result with Content. Replace by value (ReplaceAllOccurrences, ReplaceFirstOccurrence, ReplaceNthOccurrence), by position (ReplaceAnyItemAtPosition, ReplaceAnyItemAtPositions), by section (ReplaceSection puts one item, ReplaceSectionByMany splices several) or by a condition (ReplaceItemsW). The ...ByMany forms take a list of replacements: used in order, or round-robin in the XT forms. Text is compared with case, and a position outside the list is skipped without an error. AllOccurrencesReplaced is the one method that leaves the object alone and returns a changed copy.
classes.example:
o1.ReplaceAllOccurrences(2, 9)
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ 1, 9, 3, 9, 1 ]
o1.ReplaceFirstOccurrence(1, 0)
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ 0, 9, 3, 9, 1 ]
o1.ReplaceSectionByMany(2, 4, [7, 8])
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ 0, 7, 8, 1 ]

classes.name: stzListSections
classes.brief: Cuts sections out of a list by positions or by start and length, and returns the parts outside a section.
classes.description: Build one with new stzListSections(aList) or over a stzList object; it keeps its own copy. A section is named by its first and last positions (Section), a range by its start and length (Range, Ranges); an anti-section is whatever lies outside. Positions count from 1; negative ones count from the end, and out-of-range ones are clipped, not refused. Section answers a flat list, Range answers a list wrapped one level deeper. classes.name: stzListSorter
classes.brief: Orders a list and answers questions about its order: sorting, reversing, ranking, the extremes and the median.
classes.description: A sorter is built over a list with new stzListSorter(aList) or StzListSorterQ(aList); stzList has its own Sort methods and does not build one. It works on its own copy of the list, so the list you passed is never changed. The verbs (SortInAscending, SortInDescending, SortBy..., Reverse) reorder the held list in place and return nothing, the Q form returning the sorter so calls chain; the past-tense forms (SortedInAscending, SortedBy, Reversed) return a sorted copy and leave the sorter alone. Read the held list with Content. Numbers sort by value and come before texts, which sort by character code, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji texts are ordered by code point and a capital letter comes before a small one. Min, Max, Median and the Nth forms compare numbers only and answer 0 for a list of texts. SortBy takes a text expression where @item is the current item: len(@item) works, while an expression using lower() or upper() as the key does not order alphabetically. Ranks and positions count from 1.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.SortedInAscending() )
#--> [ 1, 2, 5, 7, 9 ]
? @@( o1.Ranked() )
#--> [ 3, 2, 5, 1, 4 ]
? o1.NthLargest(2)
#--> 7
o1.SortInDescending()
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ 9, 7, 5, 2, 1 ]
o2 = new stzListSorter([ "שלום", "אבא", "בית" ])
? @@( o2.Ranked() )
#--> [ 3, 1, 2 ]
o3 = new stzListSorter([ "b😀", "a😀", "😀" ])
? @@( o3.Ranked() )
#--> [ 2, 1, 3 ]

classes.name: stzListSplits
classes.brief: Cuts a list into parts: at an item, at positions, before or after one, into n parts, into parts of n items, by a condition or at a pace.
classes.description: It is the cutting helper of stzList, which builds one over itself for its Split, SplitXT, SplittedXT, SplittedAsSectionsXT and SplittedAtPositions methods; build one with new stzListSplits when you only need to cut. It works on its own copy, so a stzList passed in is never changed. The answer is a list of parts, each part a list. Unlike the split of a text, a cut item is not thrown away: it is kept and starts the next part, and a cut at position 1 or past the end adds no empty part. A verb (Split, SplitAt, SplitBefore ...) cuts the held list in place and returns nothing, so read Content afterwards, its Q form returning the splitter for chaining; the Splitted forms return the parts and leave the splitter alone. SplitXT and SplittedXT take the options in one argument (a position, a list of positions, or a pair such as [ :After, 3 ] or [ :ToNParts, 3 ]), and SplittedAsSectionsXT answers the [ first, last ] positions of the parts. A number is always read as a position, never as an item, so a list of numbers cannot be cut at one of its items. SplitAfter with an item cuts only after its last occurrence. A pace of 0 in SplitAtPacer never ends.

classes.name: stzListStringify
classes.brief: Writes a list out as text: as Ring code, with every item a text, joined with a separator, or converted between numbers and texts and in case.
classes.description: It is the writing-out helper of stzList, which builds one over itself for its Stringify, ToListInAString and ToListInAStringInShortForm methods; build one with new stzListStringify when you only need a text form. It works on its own copy, so a stzList passed in is never changed. A verb (Stringify, StringifyLists, StringifyObjects, Singlify) converts the held list in place and returns nothing, its Q form returning the stringifier for chaining; the past-tense forms (Stringified, ListsStringified, ObjectsStringified, Singlified) and the others (Lowercased, Uppercased, NumbersToStrings, StringsToNumbers, Join, ToCode) return the result and leave the stringifier alone. A number with decimals is written with two of them: 2.5 reads 2.50. StringsToNumbers raises on a text that is not numeric, and Join turns a sublist into an empty text. An object is written as the name of its variable, which is @noname when it has none. Hebrew, Arabic and emoji items are texts like any other.
classes.example:
? o1.ToCode()
#--> [ "a", 12, 2.50, [ 1, "b" ] ]
? @@( o1.Stringified() )
#--> [ "a", "12", "2.50", '[ 1, "b" ]' ]
o2 = new stzListStringify([ "a", "b", 3, "c" ])
? o2.Join("-")
#--> a-b-3-c
o3 = new stzListStringify([ 3, 4, 5, 6 ])
? o3.ToListInAStringInShortForm()
#--> 3:6
o4 = new stzListStringify([ 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 ])
? @@( o4.Singlified() )
#--> [ 1, 2, 1 ]
o5 = new stzListStringify([ "12", "3.5", 4 ])
? @@( o5.StringsToNumbers() )
#--> [ 12, 3.50, 4 ]
o6 = new stzListStringify([ "שלום", "😀", "x" ])
? o6.Join("|")
#--> שלום|😀|x

classes.name: stzListTrimmer
classes.brief: Trims a list: empty items at its ends, a given item at its ends, blank texts throughout, runs of blanks, or everything past a size.
classes.description: Build one with new stzListTrimmer(aList) or over a stzList object; it keeps its own copy, so what you passed in is not changed, and Content gives the result. Each verb that changes the list has a passive twin that returns a trimmed copy instead (Trim and Trimmed, Compact and Compacted ...). Empty, for Trim, TrimLeft and TrimRight, means the number 0, an empty or blank text, an empty sublist or a false object, so a list of numbers loses its zeros at the ends; Compact, Squeeze and StripNulls look at texts and sublists only. The Q forms (TrimQ, CompactQ ...) return the trimmer to chain on.

classes.name: stzListWalker
classes.brief: Plans walks over a list: answers the positions to visit, forward, backward, in a zigzag, by a condition, by a step or between two positions.
classes.description: It is the walking helper of stzList, which builds one over itself for its WalkNForward, WalkNBackward, WalkW, WalkUntil, WalkWhile and WalkZigZag methods; build one with new stzListWalker when you only need the plan of a walk. It never changes the list, so a stzList passed in stays intact. Every Walk method answers positions counted from 1, in the order the walk visits them, never the items: read the items with the positions, or use the XT forms that take :WalkedItems. The condition methods (WalkW, WalkUntil, WalkWhen, WalkWhile) take a test written with @item for the current item. The positions of WalkBetween and WalkFromTo are not clipped to the list. A walk whose step is 0 (WalkNForward, WalkNBackward, WalkForthAndBack, WalkZigZag) never ends. AddWalker, Walkers and Walker keep a registry of named stzWalker objects (a start, an end and the steps to repeat) beside the plans: it belongs to this one walker object, a copy of the object carries its own, names are folded to lowercase, and Walker answers a copy of the registered object. WalkAccumulating is a plain map, not a running total.

classes.name: stzLLMAgent
classes.brief: Holds a model-backed agent that proposes candidates and can never commit an effect on its own.
classes.description: It has the same shape as stzPIAgent but its body is a stzLLMFunction, and its capability set is inference only: HoldsEffectful answers 0 whatever is done to it, so the agent graph and the guardrails treat it as an llm_actor that a guarded pi-actor must admit before anything happens. Propose returns the model function's answer as a candidate. Documented and run here with a seeded answer, so no model is loaded and nothing is called over a network.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzLLMAgent("summarizer") o2 = new stzLLMFunction("sum")
classes.example:
o2.SetPrompt("summarize: {input}")
o2.Budget(2)
o2.SeedAnswer("hello world", "a greeting")
o1.SetSkillFrom(o2)
? o1.Propose("hello world")
#--> a greeting
? o1.HoldsEffectful()
#--> 0
? o1.Kind()
#--> llm_actor

classes.name: stzLLMFunction
classes.brief: Wraps a language-model call as a typed function: the reply validates as the declared type within a budget, or the call refuses.
classes.description: Declare a prompt with {input}, a return type (number, boolean, one of, free text or a whole record) and a mandatory Budget. Call_ then answers a value of that type or raises an error: no unvalidated text escapes. A reply that fails is retried inside the same budget, and the first attempt is greedy while retries draw again. Validated answers are memoized by content hash, so the same input is free and deterministic the second time. For a structured return the schema also gives the model a prompt clause and, when the engine allows, a grammar that fixes the shape of the reply; a grammar never fixes a value or the truth, so the court still checks bands. UseResponder and SeedAnswer let it run with no model for tests, and say so in Why. The object has no capability beyond mapping text to a typed value.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzLLMFunction("classify-mood"); o1.SetPrompt("Positive or negative? {input}"); o1.ReturnsOneOf([ "positive", "negative" ]) o1.Budget(5); o1.SeedAnswer("What a lovely day", "positive")
classes.example:
? o1.Call_("What a lovely day")
#--> positive
? o1.CallsMade()
#--> 0
? o1.HasSchema()
#--> 0

classes.name: stzLlmSandbox
classes.brief: Stands in for a language-model port in tests, replaying seeded answers and counting calls, with no model and no network.
classes.description: A port is any object with a Complete method that answers a hash list with ok, text and from. This one gives three things a real model cannot: determinism (a seeded prompt always gets the same answer), a measurable cost (the number of calls and an approximate token count, so a budget becomes an assertion) and offline use. A seeded answer is tried first, then a fragment rule, then the fallback; in strict mode, the default, anything else raises an error. It cannot reproduce the quality of a real model: use it for the shape of a pipeline, prompts assembled and answers parsed, and judge quality against the real thing separately. Its state lives in a shared table, so a copy of the object sees the same answers and calls.
classes.example:
o1.SeedAnswer("What is 2+2?", "4")
o1.WhenPromptContains("summarise", "A short summary.")
? o1.Complete("What is 2+2?")[:text]
#--> 4
? o1.Complete("Please summarise this")[:from]
#--> scripted
? o1.NumberOfCalls()
#--> 2
? o1.WasAskedAbout("SUMMARISE")
#--> 1

classes.name: stzLoadDriver
classes.brief: Drives real concurrent load at a server with separate processes and measures the response time clients see, to show the knee of the curve.
classes.description: The knee, response time exploding as throughput nears its ceiling, is the signature of queueing, and queueing needs concurrent arrivals that a serial in-process harness can never produce. The driver spawns a target stzAppServer as a child, or aims at a server already running, then runs a number of driver processes at once, each firing its requests one after another and printing every duration it observed, wait in the accept queue included. It is a closed-loop model: a driver fires its next request when the previous answers. DriveWith gives one level, Curve several, Explain narrates the knee. Spawning processes was not run for this reference; the settings, AimAt, WaitReady against a closed port and Explain were.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzLoadDriver() o1.SetBusyMs(5) o1.SetRequestsPerDriver(10) o1.AimAt("127.0.0.1", 1)
classes.example:
? o1.Port()
#--> 1
? @@( o1.CurveRows() )
#--> [ ]
? o1.WaitReady(200)
#--> 0
? o1.Explain()[1]
#--> Driven load -- target 127.0.0.1:1, D ~5ms CPU/request, 0 level(s).
? o1.Destroy().Port()
#--> 1

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a load driver with a reactor, the Ring executable found from the command line and the path of stzBase, and default settings.
methods.returns: nothing; the object is built and no process is started
notes: the defaults are a target cost of 3 ms per request, 30 requests per driver, the path /work and a 120000 ms lifetime for the target; StzLoadDriver builds the same object

methods.name: SetBusyMs
methods.brief: Sets how many milliseconds of CPU the spawned target burns for each request, the service demand under study.

parameters.name: pnMs
parameters.role: the cost in milliseconds, 0 or more

methods.returns: the driver itself, so calls chain
notes: it takes effect when SpawnTarget starts the target

methods.name: SetRequestsPerDriver
methods.brief: Sets how many requests each driver process fires one after another.

parameters.name: pnM
parameters.role: the number of requests, 1 or more

methods.returns: the driver itself, so calls chain

methods.name: SetPath
methods.brief: Sets the path the drivers request.

parameters.name: pcPath
parameters.role: the path, such as /work

methods.returns: the driver itself, so calls chain
notes: the target the driver spawns serves /work and /health

methods.name: SetTtlMs
methods.brief: Sets how long the spawned target lives before it ends itself, so an orphan cannot outlive its use.

parameters.name: pnMs
parameters.role: the lifetime in milliseconds, 1000 or more

methods.returns: the driver itself, so calls chain

methods.name: AimAt
methods.brief: Points the drivers at a server that is already running, instead of spawning one.

parameters.name: pcHost
parameters.role: the host name or address

parameters.name: pnPort
parameters.role: the port

methods.returns: the driver itself, so calls chain
notes: after it Destroy has no process to kill

methods.name: SpawnTarget
methods.brief: Starts a child Ring process running a small stzAppServer whose /work handler burns CPU, and waits until it answers /health.

parameters.name: pnPort
parameters.role: the port to listen on, or 0 to pick one from the wall clock between 37000 and 37899

methods.returns: TRUE when the child answered its readiness probe within 15 seconds, FALSE otherwise
notes: the target ends itself after the lifetime set by SetTtlMs
warnings: not run: it starts a child process, listens on a local port and writes a generated script to base/perf/.stzloadtarget_gen.ring

methods.name: Port
methods.brief: Returns the port of the target.
methods.returns: a number; 0 before SpawnTarget or AimAt

methods.name: WaitReady
methods.brief: Asks the target's /health until it answers 200, for up to a given time.

parameters.name: pnTimeoutMs
parameters.role: how long to keep asking, in milliseconds

methods.returns: TRUE as 1 when it answered in time, FALSE as 0 otherwise
notes: aimed at a local port where nothing listens it answered 0 after the timeout, here 300 ms; the child needs a moment to load stzBase and bind, hence the retries

methods.name: DriveWith
methods.brief: Fires one load level, a number of driver processes at once, and measures the response time each client sees.

parameters.name: pnDrivers
parameters.role: how many driver processes to run at the same time

methods.returns: a hash list with the keys drivers, requests, x, rmeanms, rp50ms, rp95ms and wallms: the throughput in requests per second and the response times in milliseconds
notes: closed loop: each driver fires its next request when the previous answers, and the wait for the accept queue is counted, which a server-side timer cannot see; the row is also appended to CurveRows
warnings: a call with no target raises error stzLoadDriver: no target -- SpawnTarget() or AimAt() first; the real run was not run: it spawns one Ring process for each driver and writes a generated script to base/perf/.stzloaddriver_gen.ring

methods.name: Curve
methods.brief: Runs several load levels in turn and returns the response-time against throughput rows.

parameters.name: paLevels
parameters.role: the numbers of drivers to try, such as [ 1, 6 ]

methods.returns: a list of the rows DriveWith gives, one for each level
notes: the values are live measurements, so a guard should assert ranges and signs and not exact values
warnings: not run: each level spawns driver processes; it clears the rows kept so far before it starts

methods.name: CurveRows
methods.brief: Returns the rows gathered so far by DriveWith and Curve.
methods.returns: a list of hash lists; [ ] before any level was driven

methods.name: Explain
methods.brief: Returns the curve as lines of text: a header, one line per level, and a closing sentence about the knee when there are two levels or more.
notes: with no level driven it is the header alone; for levels of 1 and 6 drivers reading 100 and 160 requests per second and 10 and 37 ms it says 6x the drivers bought 1.6x the throughput at 3.7x the response time, checked by hand

methods.name: Show
methods.brief: Prints the narrated curve to the console, one line per line.
notes: it prints with the ? statement

methods.name: Destroy
methods.brief: Kills the target child that SpawnTarget started.
methods.returns: the driver itself, so calls chain
notes: it does nothing for a target the driver did not spawn, such as one given to AimAt

classes.name: stzLocale
classes.brief: Holds a locale such as fr-FR and answers its country, language, script, currency, week days, time patterns and number symbols.
classes.description: A stzLocale is a locale code kept as text with an underscore (fr_FR). Build it from a code, a language name, a country name, a hash of parts, :System or :Default; the library's own tables then answer the facts: CountryName, LanguageName, CurrencyInfo, the first day of the week (monday for fr-FR, sunday for en-US, saturday for ar-EG), time patterns, DecimalPoint and GroupSeparator. The week methods come in three faces, English, native (the locale's own language) and the abbreviation and one-letter symbol of each, all counted from the locale's first day. A locale the tables do not know answers empty text. The case methods are Unicode-wide and follow the Turkish and Azerbaijani dotted and dotless i. Day names exist only for ten languages; the others answer English.
classes.example:
? o1.CountryName()
#--> france

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds the locale from a code such as fr-FR or ar_Arab_TN, a language or country name, a hash of parts, :System or :Default.

parameters.name: pLocale
parameters.role: a locale code with - or _ between its parts, a language name such as French, a country name such as France, [ :Language = ..., :Script = ..., :Country = ... ], :System or :Default

notes: a language code alone completes to its default country (fr gives fr_FR); :System gives the C locale and :Default gives the library's default locale (en_US when probed); the code is stored with an underscore
warnings: a code the library does not know (xx-YY) is kept as given and every lookup answers empty text; a hash with none of the three keys raises Can't create the stzLocale object!; a number builds an empty locale without an error

methods.name: Abbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the locale code as normalised text, with an underscore, such as fr_FR.
notes: the Content form answers the same

methods.name: Value
methods.brief: Returns the locale code as normalised text, such as fr_FR.

methods.name: bcp47Abbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the locale code with a hyphen between its parts, the BCP 47 spelling, such as fr-FR.

methods.name: CountryNumber
methods.brief: Returns the library's number for the locale's country, as text; 0 when the country is not known.
methods.returns: a string of digits such as 74, or 0
notes: the number belongs to the library's own country table

methods.name: CountryShortAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the two-letter country code, such as FR or US.
notes: empty when the country is not known; the CountryAbbreviation form answers the same

methods.name: CountryLongAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter country code, such as FRA or USA.
notes: empty when the country is not known

methods.name: CountryPhoneCode
methods.brief: Returns the international dialling code of the country, with its plus sign, such as +33.
notes: empty when the country is not known

methods.name: CountryName
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the country in lowercase, with underscores for spaces, such as united_states.
notes: empty when the country is not known; the CountryNativeName form gives the same English name, not a native one

methods.name: LanguageNumber
methods.brief: Returns the library's number for the locale's language, as text.
methods.returns: a string of digits such as 37
notes: the number belongs to the library's own language table

methods.name: LanguageName
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the locale's language in lowercase, such as french.
notes: taken from the language code, and from the country when the code names no language; empty for an unknown locale

methods.name: LanguageNativeName
methods.brief: Returns the name of the language written in that language, such as Français.
notes: falls back to the English name when no native name is known

methods.name: LanguageAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the language code of the locale, such as fr.

methods.name: LanguageShortAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the two-letter language code of the locale, such as fr.

methods.name: LanguageLongAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter language code of the locale, such as fra.

methods.name: ScriptNumber
methods.brief: Returns the library's number for the locale's script, as text, such as 7 for Latin.
methods.returns: a string of digits; 0 means common
notes: a script written in the code wins (ar_Arab_TN gives 1); otherwise the script of the language's own name is taken, so fr-FR gives Latin and ru-RU Cyrillic, and ja-JP gives Han, the script of its Japanese name; the ScriptCode form answers the same

methods.name: ScriptName
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the locale's script in lowercase, such as latin or arabic.
methods.returns: a string such as latin or arabic
notes: follows ScriptNumber; the Script form answers the same

methods.name: ScriptAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the four-letter script code, such as Latn or Arab.
methods.returns: a string such as Latn or Arab; Zyyy for common
notes: follows ScriptNumber

methods.name: CurrencyName
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the country's currency with only its first letter capitalised, such as Euro.
methods.returns: a string such as United states dollar
notes: empty when the country is not known; the Currency form answers the same

extensions.name: CurrencyXT
extensions.adds: the extended form: more parameters than the base method

methods.name: CurrencyNativeName
methods.brief: Returns the currency name in lowercase with spaces, such as euro or united states dollar.
notes: still the English name: the library holds no native currency names

methods.name: CurrencyAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter ISO code of the country's currency, such as EUR.
notes: empty when the country is not known

methods.name: CurrencyISOSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter ISO code of the country's currency, such as USD.

methods.name: CurrencySymbol
methods.brief: Returns the currency sign of the country, such as the euro sign or $.
notes: the CurrencyNativeSymbol form answers the same

methods.name: CurrencyNativeSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the currency sign as written in the country, such as the euro sign or £.
notes: the same sign as CurrencySymbol

methods.name: CurrencyFractionalUnit
methods.brief: Returns the name of the currency's subunit, such as Cent, Sen or Piastre.
notes: empty when the country is not known; the CurrencyFraction form answers the same

methods.name: CurrencyBase
methods.brief: Returns how many subunits make one unit of the currency, such as 100.
notes: empty text when the country is not known

methods.name: CurrencyInfo
methods.brief: Returns the currency facts as one hash: name, native name, abbreviation, symbols, fractional unit and base.
methods.returns: a hash with the keys name, nativename, abbreviation, symbol, nativesymbol, isosymbol, fractionalunit, fraction and base
notes: every value is empty text for an unknown country

methods.name: amText
methods.brief: Returns the text that marks the morning in a 12-hour time, AM.
notes: takes nothing from the locale: fr-FR and en-US both answer AM

methods.name: pmText
methods.brief: Returns the text that marks the afternoon in a 12-hour time, PM.
notes: takes nothing from the locale: fr-FR and en-US both answer PM

methods.name: TimeShortFormat
methods.brief: Returns the locale's short time pattern, such as HH:mm or h:mm AP.
notes: 24-hour for fr-FR, 12-hour with AP for en-US

methods.name: TimeLongFormat
methods.brief: Returns the locale's long time pattern, with seconds and a zone mark, such as HH:mm:ss t.
notes: 24-hour for fr-FR, 12-hour with AP for en-US

methods.name: TimeNarrowFormat
methods.brief: Returns the locale's narrow time pattern, such as HH:mm or h:mm AP.
notes: the same as the short pattern in the locales tried

methods.name: TimeFormat
methods.brief: Returns the locale's time pattern of one kind: long, short or narrow.

parameters.name: cType
parameters.role: the kind of pattern: :Long, :Short or :Narrow

notes: an unknown kind answers the long pattern

methods.name: ToStzTime
methods.brief: Returns a stzTime object made from a time text such as 14:30:00.

parameters.name: cTime
parameters.role: the time text, as hh:mm:ss

notes: ignores the locale: the same object comes back for every locale

methods.name: ToTimeAsString
methods.brief: Returns a time text written in the chosen format.

parameters.name: cTime
parameters.role: the time text, as hh:mm:ss

parameters.name: cFormat
parameters.role: :Default, :Long, :Short or :Narrow, the locale's formats; any other text is used as a format of HH, hh, h, mm, ss, zzz and AP

notes: the time-zone mark of a long format is left out: a stzTime holds no zone

methods.name: ToTimeAsLongString
methods.brief: Returns a time text in the locale's long time format.

parameters.name: cTime
parameters.role: the time text, as hh:mm:ss

methods.name: ToTimeAsShortString
methods.brief: Returns a time text in the locale's short time format.

parameters.name: cTime
parameters.role: the time text, as hh:mm:ss

methods.name: ToTimeAsNarrowString
methods.brief: Returns a time text in the locale's narrow time format.

parameters.name: cTime
parameters.role: the time text, as hh:mm:ss

methods.name: DaysOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the seven English day names, in lowercase, starting from the locale's first day of the week.
notes: fr-FR starts on monday, en-US on sunday, ar-EG on saturday

methods.name: NativeDaysOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the seven day names in the locale's language, starting from its first day of the week.
notes: English names come back for a language the library has no day names for (Japanese, Chinese, Hindi, Swahili); French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Turkish, Arabic, Persian and Dutch have them

methods.name: NthDayOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the nth day of the locale's week, in lowercase, counting from its first day.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the position in the week, from 1 to 7

notes: day 1 is monday for fr-FR and saturday for ar-EG
warnings: raises an error for a position outside 1 to 7, and that error is R3 because the library function that builds the message does not exist

methods.name: FirstDayOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the first day of the locale's week, in lowercase.
notes: monday for fr-FR, sunday for en-US, saturday for ar-EG

methods.name: LastDayOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the English name of the last day of the locale's week, in lowercase.
notes: sunday for fr-FR, saturday for en-US

methods.name: NthNativeDayOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the nth day name of the locale's week in its own language, counting from its first day.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the position in the week, from 1 to 7

notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: FirstNativeDayOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the name of the first day of the locale's week in its own language.
notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: LastNativeDayOfWeek
methods.brief: Returns the name of the last day of the locale's week in its own language.
notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: NthDayOfWeekAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter English abbreviation of the nth day of the locale's week, such as Tue.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the position in the week, from 1 to 7

notes: counted from the locale's first day

methods.name: NthDayOfWeekNativeAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the abbreviation, in the locale's language, of the nth day of its week, such as Mar for Mardi.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the position in the week, from 1 to 7

notes: English abbreviations when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: FirstDayOfWeekAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter English abbreviation of the first day of the locale's week.

methods.name: FirstNativeDayOfWeekAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the abbreviation, in the locale's language, of the first day of its week, such as Lun.
notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: LastDayOfWeekAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the three-letter English abbreviation of the last day of the locale's week.

methods.name: LastNativeDayOfWeekAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the abbreviation, in the locale's language, of the last day of its week, such as Dim.
notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: NativeLastDayOfWeekAbbreviation
methods.brief: Returns the abbreviation, in the locale's language, of the last day of its week, such as Dim.
notes: the same as the other spelling

methods.name: NthDayOfWeekSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the one-letter English symbol of the nth day of the locale's week, such as T for tuesday.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the position in the week, from 1 to 7

notes: counted from the locale's first day

methods.name: NthDayOfWeekNativeSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the narrow symbol, in the locale's language, of the nth day of its week, such as M for Mardi.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the position in the week, from 1 to 7

notes: English symbols when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: FirstDayOfWeekSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the one-letter English symbol of the first day of the locale's week.

methods.name: FirstDayOfWeekNativeSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the narrow symbol, in the locale's language, of the first day of its week, such as L for Lundi.
notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: LastDayOfWeekSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the one-letter English symbol of the last day of the locale's week.

methods.name: LastDayOfWeekNativeSymbol
methods.brief: Returns the narrow symbol, in the locale's language, of the last day of its week, such as D for Dimanche.
notes: English when the library has no day names for the language

methods.name: DecimalPoint
methods.brief: Returns the character that separates the whole part from the decimals, such as , for fr-FR and . for en-US.
notes: the character comes from the locale's number conventions

methods.name: Exponential
methods.brief: Returns the letter that introduces the exponent in scientific notation, e.
notes: the same for every locale

methods.name: GroupSeparator
methods.brief: Returns the character that groups thousands, such as a space for fr-FR, a comma for en-US and a dot for de-DE.
notes: the GroupSeperator form answers the same

methods.name: NegativeSign
methods.brief: Returns the sign written before a negative number, -.
notes: the same for every locale

methods.name: PositiveSign
methods.brief: Returns the sign written before a positive number, +.
notes: the same for every locale

methods.name: Percent
methods.brief: Returns the percent sign, %.
notes: the same for every locale

methods.name: StringUppercased

parameters.name: pcStr

notes: the ToUppercase, Uppercase and Upper forms answer the same; anything but a text raises an error

methods.name: CharUppercased
methods.brief: Returns one character in capitals, and empty text when the argument is not one character.

parameters.name: pcChar
parameters.role: the character to convert

methods.returns: a string; empty when not a single character

methods.name: StringIsUppercased
methods.brief: TRUE if uppercasing the text changes nothing, so it holds no small letter of any script.

parameters.name: pcStr
parameters.role: the text to test

notes: the StringIsUppercase form answers the same; an empty text answers TRUE

methods.name: CharIsUppercased
methods.brief: TRUE if uppercasing the character changes nothing, so digits and symbols answer TRUE.

parameters.name: pcChar
parameters.role: the character to test

methods.returns: TRUE or FALSE; nothing when the argument is not one character

methods.name: StringTitlecased
methods.brief: Returns the text in title case: every word capitalised in English, the first letter only in other languages.

parameters.name: pcStr

notes: the other letters are lowercased; the ToTitleCase form answers the same

methods.name: StringIsTitlecased
methods.brief: TRUE if putting the text in title case changes nothing.

parameters.name: pcStr
parameters.role: the text to test

methods.name: StringFoldcased
methods.brief: Returns the Unicode case-folded text, for comparing texts whatever their case: Straße gives strasse.

parameters.name: pcStr
parameters.role: the text to fold

notes: the ToFoldcase form answers the same; anything but a text raises an error

methods.name: CharFoldcased
methods.brief: Returns one character case-folded, and nothing when the argument is not one character.

parameters.name: pcChar
parameters.role: the character to fold

methods.returns: a string; nothing when not a single character

methods.name: StringIsfoldcased
methods.brief: TRUE if case folding the text changes nothing.

parameters.name: pcStr

notes: the StringIsFoldcase form answers the same

methods.name: CharIsFoldcased
methods.brief: TRUE if case folding the character changes nothing.

methods.brief: Returns the text lowercased with the first letter of every word, after a space, tab or line break, capitalised.

parameters.name: pcStr

methods.name: StringIsCapitalised
methods.brief: TRUE if capitalising the text changes nothing.

methods.name: MeasurementSystem
methods.brief: Returns the name of the measurement system the locale uses, such as metric or imperial, as library text.
methods.returns: a string such as metricsytem, imperialussystem or imperialuksystem
notes: the metric name is spelled metricsytem as shipped; en-US gives imperialussystem and en-GB imperialuksystem

methods.name: pvtCurrencyXT
methods.brief: Returns one piece of currency text for the locale's country: its ISO code, native symbol or native name.

parameters.name: pcTypeOfSymbol
parameters.role: which piece: :ISOSymbol, :NativeSymbol or :NativeName

methods.returns: the piece of text asked for
notes: the public Currency methods call it; status internal

classes.name: stzLog
classes.brief: Keeps a structured, leveled log in memory that you can filter, query by field and render as text or JSON.
classes.description: A log is a stream of entries, each a hash-list with seq, ts (epoch milliseconds), level, category, message and fields. The levels run trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal; the threshold (info by default) drops anything below it. Write with Record or the shortcuts Info, Warn and the rest, which return the log so writes chain; read with Entries, EntriesOfLevel, Where, OfTrace and Since; render with AsText, AsJson and OtelJson, or write to a file. A cap keeps only the newest entries.
classes.example:
o1.Info("build started")
o1.Record(:error, "compile failed", [ [ :part, "api" ], [ :code, 2 ] ])
o1.Debug("hidden")
? o1.NumberOfEntries()
#--> 2
? o1.CountOfLevel(:error)
#--> 1
? @@( o1.LastEntry()[:message] )
#--> "compile failed"
? @@( o1.Where(:part, "api")[1][:fields] )
#--> [ [ "part", "api" ], [ "code", 2 ] ]
? @@( o1.Level() )
#--> "info"

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds an empty log for one category, with the threshold info, no echo and no cap on the entries kept.

parameters.name: pcName
parameters.role: the category stamped on every entry, such as deploy

methods.name: Name
methods.brief: Returns the category the log was built with, which every entry carries.

methods.name: SetLevel
methods.brief: Sets the lowest level that is recorded, so that anything below it is dropped from now on.

parameters.name: pcLevel
parameters.role: one of trace, debug, info, warn, error or fatal, in any case

notes: entries already recorded stay
warnings: raises an error naming the unknown level for any other text, and keeps the old level

extensions.name: SetLevelQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Level
methods.brief: Returns the lowest level that is recorded, in lowercase.
methods.returns: a text such as info; info on a new log

methods.name: SetEcho
methods.brief: Turns on or off the printing of each entry to the console as it is recorded.

parameters.name: pbOn
parameters.role: 1 to print every new entry, 0 to keep quiet

notes: the printed line is the same as one line of AsText

extensions.name: SetEchoQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: SetCap
methods.brief: Sets how many entries the log keeps, evicting the oldest first; 0 means no limit.

parameters.name: pnCap
parameters.role: the most entries to keep, or 0 for no limit

notes: the cap is applied when the next entry is recorded, so lowering it does not trim at once

extensions.name: SetCapQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Record
methods.brief: Records one entry with a level, a message and structured fields, unless the level is below the threshold.

parameters.name: pcLevel
parameters.role: the level of the entry, such as warn

parameters.name: pcMsg
parameters.role: the message text

parameters.name: paFields
parameters.role: a list of key and value pairs such as [ [ :part, "api" ] ], or [ ] for none

methods.returns: the log itself, so writes chain
notes: each entry is a hash-list with seq, ts, level, category, message and fields; inside a trace scope a traceId field is added

classes.name: stzLogisticRegression
classes.brief: Fits a binary logistic regression on numeric features and answers the probability of the second label.
classes.description: Training runs in the engine by gradient descent for the number of epochs given. The model needs exactly two labels; the one that appears second in the training set is the positive class. Probability answers its chance, Classify applies the 0.5 threshold, and Why states the weights behind the last answer. Scale features of very different sizes first. TrainingAccuracy scores the model on its own training examples, which says it learned them and not that it will generalise.
classes.example:
o1.Train(200)
? o1.Classify([8, 8])
#--> high
? o1.Classify([1, 1])
#--> low
? o1.TrainingAccuracy()
#--> 1
? o1.Probability([8, 8]) > 0.9
#--> 1

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a binary logistic regression over a training set; the set must hold exactly two labels.

parameters.name: poTrainingSet
parameters.role: a stzTrainingSet of numeric features with two labels

notes: the second label to appear is the positive class that Probability measures
warnings: raises an error naming the count when the set has one label or more than two

methods.name: TrainingSetQ
methods.brief: Returns the training set the model holds.

methods.name: SetLearningRate
methods.brief: Sets the step size of the gradient descent.

parameters.name: n
parameters.role: the learning rate, above 0

methods.returns: the model itself, so calls chain
notes: a value of 0 or less is ignored without a message

methods.name: Train
methods.brief: Fits the weights and the bias by gradient descent in the engine, for a fixed number of epochs.

parameters.name: nEpochs
parameters.role: the number of passes over the examples

methods.returns: the model itself, so calls chain
notes: training again refits from zero; with 0 epochs the weights stay 0 and every probability is 0.5
warnings: raises an error for an empty set and for an example whose width differs from the first

methods.name: Probability
methods.brief: Returns the model's probability that a feature list belongs to the positive class, the second label.

parameters.name: paFeatures
parameters.role: the numbers describing the thing to score, as many as the model was fitted on

warnings: raises an error telling to call Train first, and one naming the width when the query does not match

methods.name: Probabilities
methods.brief: Returns the probability for many feature lists in one call into the engine.

parameters.name: paRows
parameters.role: a list of feature lists, each as wide as the fitted model

methods.returns: a list of numbers, one per row; an empty list for no rows
warnings: raises an error telling to call Train first, and one naming the row of the wrong width

methods.name: Classify
methods.brief: Returns the label the model predicts: the second label when its probability reaches 0.5, else the first.

parameters.name: paFeatures
parameters.role: the numbers describing the thing to classify

warnings: raises the errors of Probability

methods.name: Weights
methods.brief: Returns the fitted weights, one per feature.
methods.returns: a list of numbers; empty before Train

methods.name: Bias
methods.brief: Returns the fitted bias, the term added to the weighted sum.

methods.name: TrainingAccuracy
methods.brief: Returns the share of the training examples the model labels correctly.
methods.returns: a number from 0 to 1; 0 before Train

methods.name: Why
methods.brief: Returns the last answer of Classify as text: the probability, the epochs, the label chosen, the weights and the bias.
methods.returns: a text; empty before the first Classify

classes.name: stzLoweringBridge
classes.brief: Turns the operations a target alone can perform into the artifact of that target: firmware source for a microcontroller, a manifest otherwise.
classes.description: The bridge is the deploy-time half of the two worlds: the scope rehearses what the development machine cannot do, and the bridge lowers those operations to real text for the target, such as digitalRead(4) for a pin read. Flashing or uploading the result is a separate act that needs the device. It holds no state.
classes.example:
? o1.ExtensionFor("esp32")
#--> .ino
? o1.ExtensionFor("linux")
#--> .txt
? len(StzFind("digitalRead(4)", o1.LowerOps([ [ "gpio", "read_pin", [ 4 ], "read pin 4" ] ], "espidf"))) > 0
#--> 1

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds the bridge, which holds no state.

methods.name: LowerOps
methods.brief: Turns rehearsed operations into the artifact text of a target: firmware source for a microcontroller, else a manifest.

parameters.name: paOps
parameters.role: a list of [ capability, verb, arguments, description ] rows

parameters.name: pcOs
parameters.role: the target's operating-system name

methods.returns: a text; for espidf, esp32, arduino and rtos a firmware sketch where read_pin gives digitalRead and write_pin gives digitalWrite, else a manifest line per operation
notes: it takes plain data and builds nothing on the device: flashing is a separate act
warnings: in firmware, an operation other than the two pin verbs becomes a comment

methods.name: Lower
methods.brief: Lowers the rehearsed operations of a scope straight into its target's artifact.

parameters.name: poScope
parameters.role: the stzSystemScope whose rehearsed operations are lowered

methods.returns: a text, as LowerOps returns; a header with no operations when none was rehearsed
notes: the target is read from the scope's operating-system name
warnings: operations done on a copy of a scope are not in the scope the part retains

methods.brief: Returns the file extension the artifact of a target takes.

parameters.name: pcOs
parameters.role: the target's operating-system name, matched without regard to case

methods.returns: a text: .ino for espidf, esp32, arduino and rtos, else .txt

classes.name: stzMailSandbox
classes.brief: Captures every message instead of sending it, so a magic link or a one-time code lands in an inbox a test can read.
classes.description: A mail port is any object with Send(to, subject, body). This sandbox is the development stand-in: free, deterministic and offline, it records what would have gone out and never delivers, so an agent set loose with only a sandbox port causes no real effect. The captured messages live in a shared sink keyed by an id, so a copy of the object, which Ring makes when it is stored in another object, reads and writes the same sink. At deploy you bind your own adapter behind the same one- method contract. It does not validate addresses or text.
classes.example:
o1.Send("aicha@example.com", "Your code", "Code 492039")
o1.Send("zin@example.com", "Hello", "Hi Zin")
? o1.Count()
#--> 2
? o1.LastTo()
#--> zin@example.com
? o1.InboxOf("aicha@example.com")[1][:body]
#--> Code 492039
? o1.IsSandbox()
#--> 1

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a mail capture sink with an empty inbox, a shared slot that copies of the object also use.

methods.name: Send
methods.brief: Captures a message that would have been sent and delivers nothing, so a test can assert on it.

parameters.name: pcTo
parameters.role: the recipient

parameters.name: pcSubject
parameters.role: the subject line

parameters.name: pcBody
parameters.role: the message text

methods.returns: the sandbox itself, so calls chain
notes: the message gets a sequence number
warnings: nothing is validated: a recipient or subject holding a line break, such as a header-injection attempt, is captured as given, so a test passes on input that a real mail adapter must refuse

methods.name: IsSandbox
methods.brief: TRUE if the object is a test double; here it always is, so the registry can refuse it in production.

methods.name: Sent
methods.brief: Returns every captured message, in order.

methods.name: Count
methods.brief: Returns how many messages are captured.

methods.name: IsEmpty
methods.brief: TRUE if nothing has been captured.

methods.name: Last
methods.brief: Returns the last captured message.
methods.returns: a hash list [ :to, :subject, :body, :seq ]; an empty list when none

methods.name: LastBody
methods.brief: Returns the body of the last captured message, such as a magic link or a one-time code.

methods.name: LastTo
methods.brief: Returns the recipient of the last captured message.

methods.name: InboxOf
methods.brief: Returns the captured messages addressed to one recipient.

parameters.name: pcTo
parameters.role: the recipient, matched exactly, case included

methods.name: Clear
methods.brief: Removes every captured message from the sink, keeping the sink itself.

extensions.name: ClearQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Show
methods.brief: Prints one line with the number of captured messages.

classes.name: stzMaterialGraph
classes.brief: Holds a surface material as a graph of operations, derives the order and the reuse, proves it, and emits the shader body.
classes.description: Declare what the material takes, colours, scalars and textures, then nodes, each an operation on named inputs, in any order, and name the output with Emits. Compile derives the emission order by topological sort, counts how many nodes read each node so a node read twice is emitted once, and proves the graph: every input resolves, no cycle, no node computed for nobody. Because the graph is an ordinary stzGraph, Affects and ImpactOf answer what a node influences. ToW emits the material-language body, ToMaterial a stzMaterialMaker and ToWGSL the shader. Today a node that reads the same node in two inputs, such as a squared value, raises at Compile. Rendering is not done here.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzMaterialGraph() o1.TakesColor(:base) o1.TakesScalar(:sharp) o1.TakesTexture(:skin) o1.AddNode(:out, [ :Op = :Mix, :In = [ :lit, :base, :rim ] ]) o1.AddNode(:tex, [ :Op = :Sample, :In = [ :skin, "@uv" ] ]) o1.AddNode(:lit, [ :Op = :Multiply, :In = [ :tex, "@lambert" ] ]) o1.AddNode(:rim, [ :Op = :Fresnel, :In = [ :sharp ] ]) o1.Emits(:out) o1.Compile()
classes.example:
? @@( o1.Order() )
#--> [ "tex", "rim", "lit", "out" ]
? o1.ToW()
#--> { let n_tex = sample(skin, @uv); let n_rim = pow(1.0 - abs(@normal.z), sharp); let n_lit = (n_tex * @lambert); @out = mix(n_lit, base, n_rim) }
? @@( o1.Affects(:tex) )
#--> [ "out", "lit" ]
? o1.ImpactOf("tex")
#--> 2
? o1.IsSound()
#--> 1

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds an empty material graph with no declared values, no nodes and no output.
notes: StzMaterialGraphQ builds the same object; the ops are listed by StzMaterialGraphOps

methods.name: TakesColor
methods.brief: Declares a colour the material takes from outside, usable as a node input by name.

parameters.name: pcName
parameters.role: the name of the colour, in any letter case

methods.returns: nothing; the name is added in lower case. TakesColorQ returns the graph for chaining
notes: the graph must be compiled again afterwards

extensions.name: TakesColorQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: TakesScalar
methods.brief: Declares a number the material takes from outside, usable as a node input by name.

parameters.name: pcName
parameters.role: the name of the scalar, in any letter case

methods.returns: nothing; the name is added in lower case. TakesScalarQ returns the graph for chaining

extensions.name: TakesScalarQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: TakesTexture
methods.brief: Declares a picture the material reads, usable as the first input of a Sample node.

parameters.name: pcName
parameters.role: the name of the texture, in any letter case

methods.returns: nothing; the name is added in lower case. TakesTextureQ returns the graph for chaining

extensions.name: TakesTextureQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: AddNode
methods.brief: Declares a node, an operation on named inputs, in any order relative to the nodes it reads.

parameters.name: pcName
parameters.role: the name of the node, unique and not the name of a declared colour, scalar or texture

parameters.name: paSpec
parameters.role: a hash list [ :Op = the operation, :In = a list of inputs ], each input a node name, a declared value, a builtin such as @uv or @normal.y, or a number

methods.returns: nothing; the node is added in lower case and the graph must be compiled again. AddNodeQ returns the graph for chaining
notes: the ops are Sample, Multiply, Add, Subtract, Mix, Smoothstep, Step, Clamp, Pow, Fract, Abs, Sqrt, Sin, Cos, Dot, OneMinus, Fresnel and Lit; a whole number input is written with .0 in the shader
warnings: an empty name raises error stzMaterialGraph.AddNode: a node needs a name; a name already used, or the name of a declared value, raises an error saying the node is declared twice or cannot shadow it; an unknown operation raises error ... is not an op, with the list of the ops; a wrong number of inputs raises error ... takes N input(s)

extensions.name: AddNodeQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Emits
methods.brief: Sets which node supplies the final colour of the material.

parameters.name: pcName
parameters.role: the name of the output node

methods.returns: nothing; the name is stored in lower case. EmitsQ returns the graph for chaining

extensions.name: EmitsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: NodeCount
methods.brief: Returns how many nodes have been declared.

methods.name: OutputNode
methods.brief: Returns the name of the node declared as the output.
methods.returns: the name as text in lower case; an empty text before Emits

methods.name: Compile
methods.brief: Derives the emission order and the reuse of the graph and proves its properties.
methods.returns: the graph itself, so calls chain
notes: the findings are an unresolved_input error for an input that is no node, no declared value and no builtin, an acyclic error for a cycle, and a dead_node warning for a node nothing reads other than the output; a graph with a cycle has an empty order
warnings: a graph with no node raises error stzMaterialGraph.Compile: no nodes declared; with no output, error ... no output -- say Emits(:node); with an output that is not a node, error ... the output node ... does not exist; a node that reads the same node in two of its inputs, such as Multiply with [ :a, :a ], raises the stzGraph error saying parallel edges are refused, because one edge is added for each input

methods.name: Order
methods.brief: Returns the nodes in the order they are emitted, derived so that a node comes after every node it reads.
methods.returns: a list of node names in lower case; [ ] after a cycle
notes: declare the nodes in any order at all
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: Uses
methods.brief: Returns how many nodes read each node.
methods.returns: a list of [ node, consumers ] pairs in declaration order; the output has 0
notes: a node read by two nodes is emitted once, as one let
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: ReuseSaved
methods.brief: Returns how many expressions the single emission of shared nodes saves over writing the graph out as a tree.
methods.returns: a number, each node's consumers beyond the first added up
notes: 0 when no node is read twice
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: Affects
methods.brief: Returns every node downstream of a node, that is every node that depends on it, directly or not.

parameters.name: pcNode
parameters.role: the node to ask about, in any letter case

methods.returns: a list of node names, the node itself not included; [ ] for an output node or an unknown name
notes: it is a reachability query on the stzGraph the compile builds
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: ImpactOf
methods.brief: Returns how many nodes depend on a node, directly or not.

parameters.name: pcNode
parameters.role: the node to ask about, in any letter case

methods.returns: a number; 0 for an output node or an unknown name
notes: the length of the list Affects gives
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: Findings
methods.brief: Returns the proofs that failed or warned, in the house finding shape.
methods.returns: a list of hash lists with rule, subject materialgraph, where material, severity and message; [ ] for a clean graph
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: IsSound
methods.brief: TRUE if the compiled graph has no finding of severity error.
notes: a dead_node warning does not make it false
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: Report
methods.brief: Returns the findings as a stzRuleReport, so the graph is judged by the same gate as code and security rules.
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first

methods.name: ToW
methods.brief: Returns the material-language body the graph emits, one let for each node in order and then the output.
methods.returns: the text, such as { let n_a = abs(1.0); @out = (n_a + 2.0) }
notes: the text can be read and debugged; the output node has no let
warnings: calling it before Compile raises error stzMaterialGraph: call Compile() first; a graph with an error finding raises error stzMaterialGraph.ToW: the graph has ERRORS

methods.name: ToMaterial
methods.brief: Builds a stzMaterialMaker with the declared colours, scalars and textures and this body, ready to give to a scene.
notes: rendering the material was not run here
warnings: the graph must have been compiled and be sound, as for ToW

methods.name: ToWGSL
methods.brief: Returns the WGSL shader of the material, by way of the material maker the graph builds.
notes: no device is needed to produce it
warnings: the graph must have been compiled and be sound, as for ToW

classes.name: stzMaterialMaker
classes.brief: Describes how a surface should look, as declared colours, scalars and textures and one fragment expression, and has the engine write the shader.
classes.description: You declare what the material takes, TakesColor, TakesScalar and TakesTexture, and write the body once as @out = expression, where the expression uses the declared names, numbers, the arithmetic operators, a whitelist of functions and the fragment builtins @normal, @position, @uv, @lambert and @color. ToWGSL has the engine transpile it to a complete shader and refuses a bad description with a message naming the offender. ParamsFrom and TexturesFrom flatten the values a scene binds. Authoring needs no GPU: only rendering the material wants hardware, and this class never renders.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzMaterialMaker o1.TakesColor(:base) o1.TakesScalar(:glow) o1.ForEachFragment('{ @out = base * (1.0 + glow * @normal.y) }')
classes.example:
? @@( o1.ColorNames() )
#--> [ "base" ]
? o1.Spec()
#--> color base
scalar glow
body { @out = base * (1.0 + glow * @normal.y) }
? len(o1.ParamsFrom([ :base = "#e0a030", :glow = 0.6 ]))
#--> 5
? left(o1.ToWGSL(), 6)
#--> struct
