methods.brief: TRUE if the text holds no character at all.

methods.name: NumberOfOccurrence
methods.brief: Returns how many times a fragment occurs in the text, never counting two occurrences that overlap.

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the fragment to count

methods.returns: a number; 0 when absent or when the fragment is empty
notes: NumberOfOccurrences is the same call; case-sensitive, and NumberOfOccurrenceCS with 0 ignores case: an in Banana banana is 4, AN is 0 and AN with the flag 0 is 4

extensions.name: NumberOfOccurrenceCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: NumberOfOccurrencesCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: Count
methods.brief: Returns how many times a fragment occurs in the text, never counting two occurrences that overlap.

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the fragment to count

methods.returns: a number; 0 when absent or when the fragment is empty
notes: CountSubString is the same call; aa in aaaa gives 2, and CountCS with the flag 0 ignores case

extensions.name: CountCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: CountSubStringCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: NumberOfSubStrings
methods.brief: Returns how many substrings the text has when every pair of start and end positions counts, repeats included.
methods.returns: a number; 0 for an empty text
notes: HowManySubStrings is the same call; n characters give n*(n+1)/2, so abc gives 6 and a 13 character text 91
warnings: NumberOfSubStringsCS with the flag 0 gives the same number: the flag changes nothing today

extensions.name: NumberOfSubStringsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: HowManySubStringsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: CountBetween
methods.brief: Raises an error today instead of counting a fragment inside a section of the text.

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the fragment meant to be counted

parameters.name: n1
parameters.role: the first position of the section

parameters.name: n2
parameters.role: the last position of the section

notes: cut the section with stzString.Section, then Count it, until this is repaired
warnings: it calls the function StringNumberOfOccurrenceCS, which does not exist, so CountBetween and CountBetweenCS raise R3 for every input; confirmed with Banana banana and with xyzxyz

extensions.name: CountBetweenCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: CountAnyChar
methods.brief: Returns how many characters of the text are one of the characters of a set.

parameters.name: pcChars
parameters.role: the characters of the set, given as one text

notes: an in Banana banana gives 10 and an empty set gives 0; Hebrew works: the letters shin lamed and final mem count 5 in שלום עולם abc

methods.name: CountLeadingChar
methods.brief: Returns how many times a character repeats at the very start of the text.

parameters.name: pcChar
parameters.role: the character

methods.returns: a number; 0 when the text starts with another character
notes: two spaces then hello gives 2; case-sensitive: xxabcxx with X gives 0
warnings: an empty text stops the Ring process with a panic in stz_string.dll instead of returning 0

methods.name: CountTrailingChar
methods.brief: Returns how many times a character repeats at the very end of the text.

parameters.name: pcChar
parameters.role: the character

methods.returns: a number; 0 when the text ends with another character
notes: xxabcxx with x gives 2
warnings: an empty text stops the Ring process with a panic in stz_string.dll instead of returning 0

methods.name: CountBetweenMarkers
methods.brief: Returns how many pairs of an opening and a closing marker the text holds.

parameters.name: pcOpenMarker
parameters.role: the text that opens a pair

parameters.name: pcCloseMarker
parameters.role: the text that closes it

notes: a(b) c(d) (e with ( and ) gives 2 because the unclosed marker is not counted; longer markers such as and work

methods.name: GraphemeCount
methods.brief: Returns how many user-perceived characters the text holds, a base letter with its accents counting as one.
notes: e followed by the combining acute accent is 1 grapheme and 2 characters

methods.name: CountMarks
methods.brief: Returns how many combining marks the text holds: accents, vowel signs and similar.
notes: a base letter with an accent gives 1; the Thai and Devanagari vowel signs count too

methods.name: CountControls
methods.brief: Returns how many control characters the text holds, such as tab and line feed.
notes: a tab followed by a line feed gives 2

methods.name: CountCjk
methods.brief: Returns how many Chinese, Japanese or Korean ideographs the text holds.
notes: the four ideographs 你好世界 give 4

methods.name: CountCyrillic
methods.brief: Returns how many Cyrillic letters the text holds.
notes: Привет мир gives 9

methods.name: CountHebrew
methods.brief: Returns how many Hebrew letters the text holds.
notes: שלום עולם abc gives 8

methods.name: CountDevanagari
methods.brief: Returns how many Devanagari characters the text holds, signs and vowel marks included.
notes: the six characters of नमस्ते give 6

methods.name: CountThai
methods.brief: Returns how many Thai characters the text holds, vowel marks included.
notes: the six characters of สวัสดี give 6

methods.name: CountOverlapping
methods.brief: Returns how many times a fragment occurs in the text, counting occurrences that overlap.

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the fragment to count

notes: aa in aaaa gives 3 where Count gives 2
warnings: CountOverlappingCS ignores its flag and always compares with case: aa in AAaa gives 1 with the flag 0 and with 1, where ignoring case would give 3

extensions.name: CountOverlappingCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: CountRegex
methods.brief: Returns how many matches a regular expression has in the text.

parameters.name: pcPattern
parameters.role: the regular expression

methods.returns: a number; 0 when nothing matches or the pattern is invalid
notes: NumberOfRegexMatches is the same call; [0-9]+ in Ab1 cD22 e3 gives 3 and [0-9] gives 4; CountRegexCS with the flag 0 ignores case, so [a-c] gives 3 against 2; the Hebrew class [א-ת]+ gives 2 words in שלום עולם abc
warnings: an invalid pattern such as [ gives 0 and no error

extensions.name: CountRegexCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: NumberOfRegexMatchesCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: CountCharsW
methods.brief: Returns how many characters satisfy a condition written in the W syntax.

parameters.name: pcExpr
parameters.role: the condition, comparing @char with a quoted character

notes: CountCharsWhere and NumberOfCharsW are the same call; @char = "2" in Ab1 cD22 e3 gives 2; @char = "ל" in שלום שלום gives 2
warnings: a Q(@char).IsLowercase() or isDigit expression counts 0 and raises no error; compare @char with a quoted character

classes.name: stzStringCrypto
classes.brief: Hashes, signs and ciphers a text: SHA-256, MD5, BLAKE3, HMAC, base64, and the classic toy ciphers.
classes.description: It is the crypto helper of stzString. Build it with StzStringCryptoQ over a text, or with new stzStringCrypto, and keep the text and the key apart: the digests are engine-backed and match the published test vectors (abc gives ba7816bf... under SHA-256). The ciphers (ROT13, Caesar, Vigenere, Atbash, ROT47, XOR, Obfuscate) are toys that hide text from a glance and are not encryption: they only move the Latin letters or the ASCII range, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji pass through unchanged, while the digests, base64 and XOR work on UTF-8 bytes. A verb without an ending (ROT13, Atbash) changes the held text and returns nothing, the form ending in -ed (ROT13ed, Atbashed, CaesarEncrypted) returns the new text and leaves the helper alone. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: editing through the helper empties the stzString that was passed in. IsEncrypted answers TRUE for almost any text today.
classes.example:
? o1.Sha256()
#--> ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad
? o1.HmacSha256("key")
#--> 9c196e32dc0175f86f4b1cb89289d6619de6bee699e4c378e68309ed97a1a6ab
o2 = StzStringCryptoQ("שלום")
? o2.Base64Encode()
#--> 16nXnNeV150=

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a crypto helper over a text, given as a string or as a stzString object.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: the text to hash or encrypt, or a stzString to wrap

notes: pass a plain text and read the result with Content; the helper is not made by stzString itself, you build it over the same text
warnings: with a stzString argument, the first in-place edit (ROT13, CaesarEncrypt, Atbash, Obfuscate...) leaves the stzString you passed reading as an empty text, while the helper keeps the right one (ROT13 and Atbash on keep me, both times)

methods.name: Content
methods.brief: Returns the text as it stands now, after any in-place cipher applied through this helper.

methods.name: NumberOfChars
methods.brief: Returns how many characters the text holds, counting an Arabic letter or an emoji as one.

methods.name: IsEmpty
methods.brief: TRUE if the text holds no character at all.

methods.name: Hash
methods.brief: Returns the 64-bit FNV-1a hash of the text, a quick fingerprint that is not secure.
notes: not for passwords or integrity checks; use Sha256 or Blake3
warnings: the value is held as a number, so the low digits above 2^53 are rounded: abc gives 16654208175385434112 where the exact hash is 16654208175385433931

methods.name: Entropy
methods.brief: Returns the Shannon entropy of the characters, in hundredths of a bit per character.
methods.returns: a number; 0 for a text of one repeated character, 158 for abc
notes: the figure is already scaled by 100, so 158 means 1.58 bits

methods.name: Sha256
methods.brief: Returns the SHA-256 digest of the text as 64 lower-case hex characters.
notes: the text is hashed as UTF-8 bytes; the digest of abc is ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad, the published test vector

methods.name: Md5
methods.brief: Returns the MD5 digest of the text as 32 lower-case hex characters.
notes: MD5 is broken as a security hash; use it only for legacy checksums. The digest of abc is 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72, the published test vector

methods.name: Blake3
methods.brief: Returns the BLAKE3 digest of the text as 64 lower-case hex characters.
notes: the digest of abc is 6437b3ac38465133ffb63b75273a8db548c558465d79db03fd359c6cd5bd9d85, the published test vector

methods.name: HmacSha256
methods.brief: Returns the keyed HMAC-SHA256 of the text as 64 hex characters, so only the key holder can reproduce it.

parameters.name: pcKey
parameters.role: the secret key, as text

methods.returns: a text of 64 hex characters; an empty text for an empty key
notes: HMAC of abc under the key key is 9c196e32dc0175f86f4b1cb89289d6619de6bee699e4c378e68309ed97a1a6ab, equal to Python hmac.new
warnings: an empty key returns an empty text instead of the HMAC under the empty key

methods.name: XorEncrypt
methods.brief: Returns the text XORed byte by byte with a repeating key, encoded as base64 so it stays text.

parameters.name: pcKey
parameters.role: the passphrase that repeats along the text, as text

methods.returns: a text in base64; an empty text for an empty key
notes: the result is base64 because raw cipher bytes are not valid UTF-8 text and the engine would drop them; the helper keeps its own text, and to undo you give the base64 result to XorDecrypt with the same key
warnings: an empty key returns an empty text; a toy cipher, not secure

methods.name: XorDecrypt
methods.brief: Returns the plain text recovered from a base64 XOR result and the same key.

parameters.name: pcKey
parameters.role: the same passphrase that was used to encrypt

methods.returns: a text; an empty text for an empty key
notes: the helper must hold the base64 text that XorEncrypt returned; Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text round trips

methods.name: Checksum
methods.brief: Returns the sum of the code points of every character, a very weak fingerprint.
notes: abc gives 294, and an emoji counts as its one code point

methods.name: ChecksumHex
methods.brief: Returns the checksum written in hexadecimal.
methods.returns: a text, such as 126 for abc
notes: the text has no 0x prefix

methods.name: Base64Encode
methods.brief: Returns the text encoded in base64 from its UTF-8 bytes.
methods.returns: a text; Base64Encoded is the same call
notes: abc gives YWJj

methods.name: Base64Decode
methods.brief: Returns the text that a base64 text stands for.
methods.returns: a text; Base64Decoded is the same call
notes: the helper must hold base64; YWJj gives abc

methods.name: ROT13
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its ROT13 form, in place, rotating each Latin letter by 13.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. ROT13Q returns the helper for chaining
notes: only A-Z and a-z move; Hebrew, Arabic and emoji pass through unchanged; applying it twice restores the text

extensions.name: ROT13Q
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: ROT13ed
methods.brief: Returns the ROT13 form of the text, leaving the helper unchanged.
notes: Hello gives Uryyb

methods.name: CaesarEncrypt
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its Caesar shift of the Latin letters, in place.

parameters.name: nShift
parameters.role: how many places each letter moves forward in the alphabet, 3 for Hello giving Khoor

notes: only A-Z and a-z move; any other script and emoji pass through unchanged; a shift of 26 changes nothing

methods.name: CaesarDecrypt
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by the Caesar shift of the same size taken backwards, in place.

parameters.name: nShift
parameters.role: the shift that was used to encrypt

notes: Khoor with 3 gives Hello; a shift of 29 is read as 3

methods.name: CaesarEncrypted
methods.brief: Returns the text with each Latin letter moved forward by a shift, leaving the helper unchanged.

parameters.name: nShift
parameters.role: how many places each letter moves forward

notes: Hello with 3 gives Khoor and with -3 gives Ebiil

methods.name: VigenereEncrypt
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its Vigenere encryption under a key word, in place.

parameters.name: pcKey
parameters.role: the key word whose letters give the successive shifts

notes: the classic ATTACKATDAWN under LEMON gives LXFOPVEFRNHR; Hebrew, Arabic and emoji pass through unchanged
warnings: an empty key leaves an empty text

methods.name: VigenereEncrypted
methods.brief: Returns the Vigenere encryption of the text under a key word, leaving the helper unchanged.

parameters.name: pcKey
parameters.role: the key word whose letters give the successive shifts

notes: ATTACKATDAWN under LEMON gives LXFOPVEFRNHR; Hello World under key gives Rijvs Uyvjn
warnings: an empty key returns an empty text

methods.name: Atbash
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its Atbash form, in place, mirroring each Latin letter in the alphabet.
notes: a becomes z and Hello becomes Svool; other scripts pass through unchanged; applying it twice restores the text

methods.name: Atbashed
methods.brief: Returns the Atbash form of the text, leaving the helper unchanged.
notes: Hello gives Svool

methods.name: ROT47
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its ROT47 form, in place, rotating the printable ASCII characters by 47.
notes: Hello gives w6==@; digits and punctuation move too; characters outside printable ASCII pass through unchanged; applying it twice restores the text

methods.name: ROT47ed
methods.brief: Returns the ROT47 form of the text, leaving the helper unchanged.
notes: Hello gives w6==@

methods.name: IsEncrypted
methods.brief: TRUE if the entropy figure of the text is above 4, which almost any text with two different characters passes.
notes: do not use it to detect encryption
warnings: answers TRUE for ab, abab and a plain English sentence, and FALSE only for a text of one repeated character or an empty one: Entropy is scaled by 100 (hundredths of a bit) and is compared with 4 as if it were in bits, so the answer cannot tell cipher text from plain text today

methods.name: Obfuscate
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its reversal XORed with the fixed key ZiN and written in base64, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. ObfuscateQ returns the helper for chaining
notes: a fixed key, so it hides text from a glance and is not encryption

extensions.name: ObfuscateQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Obfuscated
methods.brief: Returns the obfuscated form of the text, leaving the helper unchanged.
notes: Hello gives NQUiPyE=

methods.name: Deobfuscated
methods.brief: Returns the plain text hidden by an obfuscation, leaving the helper unchanged.
notes: the helper must hold the base64 text that Obfuscated returned

methods.name: Deobfuscate
methods.brief: Replaces the held base64 text by the plain text it hides, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. DeobfuscateQ returns the helper for chaining
notes: undoes Obfuscate

extensions.name: DeobfuscateQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

classes.name: stzStringDuplicates
classes.brief: Finds and removes repeated characters or repeated substrings in a text.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringDuplicates("banana"). DuplicatedChars, UniqueChars and their counts look at single characters, whole letters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji work; comparisons are case-sensitive. The Remove verbs change the text held (RemoveConsecutiveDuplicateChars collapses runs, RemoveAllDuplicateChars keeps the first of each character, RemoveDuplicateSubString keeps the first occurrence of a substring) and each has a passive twin that returns the result. Do not pass a stzString object you still need: the first in-place edit empties it. RemoveDuplicateSubString mishandles overlapping matches.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.DuplicatedChars() )
#--> [ "a", "n" ]
? o1.AllDuplicateCharsRemoved()
#--> ban
? o1.DuplicateSubStringRemoved("an")
#--> bana
o2 = new stzStringDuplicates("שלומשלום😀😀")
? o2.NumberOfUniqueChars()
#--> 6

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a duplicates helper over a text or over a stzString object.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: a text, or a stzString object, whose repeated characters or substrings are examined

notes: any other kind of value raises "Can't create stzStringDuplicates! Parameter must be a string or stzString object."
warnings: Given a stzString object, the first in-place edit (RemoveConsecutiveDuplicateChars, RemoveAllDuplicateChars, RemoveDuplicateSubString) leaves that stzString EMPTY while the helper holds the result; the passive forms and the questions do not. Pass the text, os.Content(), to be safe

methods.name: Content
methods.brief: Returns the text the helper holds, after any in-place removal made through it.

methods.name: NumberOfChars
methods.brief: Returns how many characters the text holds, counting letters and not bytes.

methods.name: IsEmpty
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is empty.

methods.name: DuplicatedChars
methods.brief: Returns the characters that occur more than once in the text, each listed once, in the order of their first appearance.
notes: "banana" gives a and n; the comparison is case-sensitive, so "Aa" has none

methods.name: HasDuplicatedChars
methods.brief: TRUE if at least one character occurs more than once in the text.

methods.name: NumberOfDuplicatedChars
methods.brief: Returns how many different characters occur more than once.
notes: "banana" gives 2, not the 3 extra letters

methods.name: UniqueChars
methods.brief: Returns the different characters of the text, each once, in the order of their first appearance.
notes: "banana" gives b, a, n; Hebrew, Arabic and emoji are single characters, and the final form ם differs from מ

methods.name: NumberOfUniqueChars
methods.brief: Returns how many different characters the text holds.

methods.name: HasConsecutiveDuplicates
methods.brief: TRUE if two equal characters stand side by side somewhere in the text.
notes: "banana" is FALSE although it repeats letters, "aabbcc" is TRUE

methods.name: RemoveConsecutiveDuplicateChars
methods.brief: Collapses each run of the same character to one, in place.
notes: "aabbcc" becomes "abc" and "banana" is unchanged

extensions.name: RemoveConsecutiveDuplicateCharsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: ConsecutiveDuplicateCharsRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text with each run of the same character reduced to one, leaving the helper unchanged.

methods.name: RemoveAllDuplicateChars
methods.brief: Keeps only the first occurrence of each character, wherever the repeats stand, in place.
notes: "banana" becomes "ban"

extensions.name: RemoveAllDuplicateCharsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: AllDuplicateCharsRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text with only the first occurrence of each character kept, leaving the helper unchanged.

methods.name: RemoveDuplicateSubString
methods.brief: Keeps the first occurrence of a substring and removes the later ones, case-sensitively, in place.

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the substring whose repeats are removed

notes: RemoveDuplicateSubStringCS(pcSubStr, 0) ignores case
warnings: Occurrences that overlap are all counted, so the removal can eat more than the repeats: "aaa" with "aa" becomes "a", and "xaaaax" with "aa" becomes "xa", losing the final x; a substring that occurs once or not at all changes nothing

extensions.name: RemoveDuplicateSubStringCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: RemoveDuplicateSubStringCSQ
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag; does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

extensions.name: RemoveDuplicateSubStringQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: DuplicateSubStringRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text with the later occurrences of a substring removed, leaving the helper unchanged.

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the substring whose repeats are removed

notes: "banana" with "an" gives "bana"
warnings: the same overlap defect

extensions.name: DuplicateSubStringRemovedCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

classes.name: stzStringEncoder
classes.brief: Turns a text into another representation of itself and back: hexadecimal, binary, octal, code points, URL and HTML escapes, regex escapes and Unicode normal forms.
classes.description: It is the encoding helper behind the encoding methods of stzString (ToHex, UrlEncoded, HtmlDecoded, NormalizedNFC...), which builds one over itself and writes the result back; reach for it directly with new stzStringEncoder(cText) or StzStringEncoderQ(cText) when you only need the encoding. The past-tense forms (UrlEncoded, HtmlDecoded, NormalizedNFC...) return the new text and leave the encoder alone, and the verbs (UrlEncode, FromHex, Reverse...) change the held text in place and return nothing, the Q form returning the encoder so calls chain. Read the result with Content. Note what each form counts: ToHex gives the UTF-8 bytes, ToCharCodes and ToOctal give Unicode code points, and ToBinary gives one group of eight digits per character, which is cut to its low eight bits above code point 255, so it is exact for Latin-1 text only. FromHex does not join UTF-8 bytes back into characters, so it round-trips ASCII only. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: an edit through an encoder empties the stzString that was passed in.
classes.example:
? o1.ToHex()
#--> 486920c3a9
? o1.UrlEncoded()
#--> Hi%20%C3%A9
? o1.ToCharCodes()
#--> 72 105 32 233
o2 = new stzStringEncoder("שלום")
? o2.UrlEncoded()
#--> %D7%A9%D7%9C%D7%95%D7%9D
? o2.ToCharCodes()
#--> 1513 1500 1493 1501
o3 = new stzStringEncoder("a😀")
? o3.ToHex()
#--> 61f09f9880
? o3.ToCharCodes()
#--> 97 128512

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds an encoder over a text, given as a string or as a stzString object.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: the text to encode or decode, or a stzString whose content is used, any other value raises an error

notes: pass a plain text and read the result with Content; stzString does it safely by writing the encoder result back with Update
warnings: with a stzString argument, the first in-place edit (UrlEncode, HtmlDecode, FromHex, Reverse, NormalizeNFC...) leaves the stzString you passed reading as an empty text; the encoder itself keeps the right text

methods.name: Content
methods.brief: Returns the text as it stands now, after the in-place edits made so far.

methods.name: NumberOfChars
methods.brief: Returns how many characters the text holds, counting an emoji or a Hebrew letter as one.

methods.name: IsEmpty
methods.brief: TRUE if the text holds no character at all.

methods.name: ToHex
methods.brief: Returns the UTF-8 bytes of the text as lower-case hexadecimal digits, two per byte, with no separator.
methods.returns: a text; empty for an empty text
notes: a Hebrew letter is two bytes and an emoji four, so the result is longer than twice the character count; ToHexQ returns a new encoder over the result

extensions.name: ToHexQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: ToHexWithPrefix
methods.brief: Returns the same hexadecimal digits as ToHex, preceded by 0x.
notes: the prefix is always added, even for an empty text

methods.name: FromHex
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by the text that hexadecimal digits spell, in place, taking each pair of digits as one character.

parameters.name: cHex
parameters.role: the hexadecimal digits, two per character, a trailing odd digit is dropped

methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. FromHexQ returns the encoder for chaining
notes: for ASCII text it round-trips with ToHex
warnings: each byte becomes its own character, so only pairs below 80 give the expected text: FromHex("c3a9") answers the two characters that spell Ã© and FromHex("d7a9d795") answers four, where ToHex of é and of a Hebrew word gave those digits; the UTF-8 bytes are not joined back into characters, so ToHex and FromHex do not round-trip for text outside ASCII

extensions.name: FromHexQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: UrlEncoded
methods.brief: Returns the text percent-encoded for a URL, each byte of a non-ASCII character as %XX in upper case.
notes: a space becomes %20 and an ampersand %26

methods.name: UrlEncode
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its percent-encoded form, in place.

methods.name: UrlDecoded
methods.brief: Returns the text with every %XX sequence turned back into its character, reading the bytes as UTF-8.
notes: decoded Hebrew, Arabic and emoji come back whole

methods.name: UrlDecode
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by its percent-decoded form, in place.

methods.name: AsciiCodes
methods.brief: Returns the Unicode code point of each character, in order.
methods.returns: a list of numbers; a list of one number per character
notes: despite its name it gives code points, not only ASCII codes: a Hebrew letter answers 1513 and an emoji 128512; Unicodes is the same call

methods.name: Unicodes
methods.brief: Returns the Unicode code point of each character, in order.
methods.returns: a list of numbers; a list of one number per character

methods.name: ToBinary
methods.brief: Returns the text as one group of eight binary digits per character, groups separated by a space.
methods.returns: a text such as 01001000 01101001 for Hi
notes: exact for Latin-1 text, so use ToHex for the bytes of other scripts
warnings: a character whose code point is above 255 is cut to its low eight bits: the Hebrew shin (1513) answers 11101001, which is also what the code point 233 answers, and an emoji (128512) answers 00000000; ToBinary is not the UTF-8 bytes either, which ToHex gives

methods.name: FromBinary
methods.brief: Replaces the held text by the characters that groups of binary digits spell, in place, one character per group.

parameters.name: _cBin_

classes.name: stzStringExtractor
classes.brief: Cuts pieces out of a text: a section, a run, a character or an occurrence of a substring, returning each piece and removing it.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringExtractor("text"). Every Extract verb answers the piece and takes it out of the text the extractor holds, which Content shows. Positions count from 1 and are in characters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji are cut by letter. A section must have its start before its end: a reversed pair kills the process or removes nothing today. Extract(substr) returns the whole text before removal, not the part removed, and ExtractCharsW raises an error after removing; see their warnings. Do not pass a stzString object you still need: the first extraction empties it.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzStringExtractor("hello world, hello moon")
classes.example:
? o1.ExtractSection(1, 5)
#--> hello
? o1.NumberOfChars()
#--> 18
? o1.ExtractLastChar()
#--> n
? o1.ExtractLast("hello")
#--> hello

classes.name: stzStringFinder
classes.brief: Finds where a fragment, a pair of bounds, a repeat, a condition or a regular expression occurs in a text, as positions or sections.
classes.description: It is the search helper of stzString, which builds one over its own engine handle for its Find methods; build one with StzStringFinderQ (or new stzStringFinder) when you only need to search. It never edits the text. Positions are 1-based and count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text answers as you read it. Find returns a list of positions and a section is a [start, end] pair. Case counts unless you call the CS form with 0. The rank-0 and absent cases are not uniform today: FindFirst and FindLast answer 0 for an absent fragment, IndexOf answers -1, and FindNth answers -1 for a rank past the last occurrence. FindBetweenAsSection is greedy (first opening bound to last closing bound): use FindBoundedByAsSections for one section per pair. The W searches ignore their case flag.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.Find("an") )
#--> [ 2, 4 ]
? @@( o1.FindAsSections("an") )
#--> [ [ 2, 3 ], [ 4, 5 ] ]
o2 = StzStringFinderQ("שלום עולם שלום")
? @@( o2.Find("שלום") )
#--> [ 1, 11 ]
o3 = StzStringFinderQ("a😀b😀")
? @@( o3.FindAllChar("😀") )
#--> [ 2, 4 ]

classes.name: stzStringFormatter
classes.brief: Changes how a text looks: its case, its alignment and padding, its white space and its repetition.
classes.description: It is the formatting helper behind the case methods of stzString (Titlecased, CaseFolded...), which builds one over itself and writes the result back; reach for it directly with new stzStringFormatter(cText) or StzStringFormatterQ(cText) when you only need the formatting. Each Apply verb and each Align, Pad, Trim, Simplify and Repeat verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the formatter, so calls chain), and the past-tense form (Uppercased, RightAligned, Trimmed...) returns the new text and leaves the formatter alone. Read the result with Content. Widths and reversals count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is handled whole. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: an edit through a formatter empties the stzString that was passed in. PaddedLeft and PaddedRight ignore their padding character; use PadLeft and PadRight.
classes.example:
? o1.Titlecased()
#--> Hello World
? "[" + o1.RightAligned(14) + "]"
#--> [   hello WORLD]
o1.PadRight(14, "*")
? o1.Content()
#--> hello WORLD***
o2 = new stzStringFormatter("שלום עולם")
? o2.NumberOfChars()
#--> 9
? o2.Reversed() = "םלוע םולש"
#--> 1
o3 = new stzStringFormatter("ab😀")
? "[" + o3.CenterAligned(7) + "]"
#--> [  ab😀  ]

classes.name: stzStringGetter
classes.brief: Reads a text without changing it: a character by position, the first, last or middle, the n first or last, the characters, n-grams.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringGetter("text"); it only reads, so a stzString passed in is never emptied. Positions count from 1 and in characters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji are read by letter. NFirstChars and NLastChars refuse a count outside the text, while NthChar forgives position 0 and a position past the end. CharNgrams and WordNgrams answer the runs of n characters or n words. BytesPerChar answers a text such as "1 4 2". NLeftChars and NRightChars should swap sides for right-to-left text and do not today, because the direction test answers TRUE for it.
classes.example:
? o1.NthChar(2)
#--> e
? o1.NLastChars(3)
#--> rld
? @@( o1.CharNgrams(3) )
#--> [ "hel", "ell", "llo", "lo ", "o W", " Wo", "Wor", "orl", "rld" ]
o2 = new stzStringGetter("a😀ب")
? o2.BytesPerChar()
#--> 1 4 2

classes.name: stzStringInserter
classes.brief: Inserts a fragment into a text: at a position, around the occurrences of another fragment, or at several positions.
classes.description: It is the insertion helper of stzString, which builds one over itself for its Insert methods; build one with StzStringInserterQ (or new stzStringInserter) when you only need to insert. Each verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the inserter so calls chain), and the Inserted form returns the new text and leaves the inserter alone. Read the result with Content. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is cut where you expect. A position out of range changes nothing without any error. Found today: InsertAfterNth, InsertAfterFirst and InsertAfterLast put the new fragment in a wrong place when the fragment they look for is absent; InsertBetweenSubStrings replaces the text between the bounds instead of inserting; InsertSubStringBetweenPositions uses only the smaller position; and the two ManyPositions verbs raise R13 for every valid list.
classes.example:
o1.InsertAfterSubString("an", "-")
? o1.Content()
#--> ban-an-a
o2 = StzStringInserterQ("שלום עולם")
o2.InsertBefore(6, "!")
? o2.Content()
#--> שלום !עולם
o3 = StzStringInserterQ("a😀b")
? o3.InsertedAfterFirst("😀", "-")
#--> a😀-b

classes.name: stzStringIO
classes.brief: Moves a text in and out: saves it to a file, loads it from one, and renders it as a JSON, CSV, XML or HTML value.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringIO("text"). ToFile (also SaveTo, ExportTo), AppendToFile and PrependToFile write the text held; FromFile (also LoadFrom) replaces it with a file's content, read as UTF-8, and raises when the file is missing. ToJSON, ToCSV, ToXML and ToHTML only return a rendering. IsFilePath, IsURL, IsEmail and IsBase64 are quick shape tests, not validations. FromClipboard is a placeholder that always raises. Use an invented path of your own when you try the file methods.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzStringIO("say " + char(34) + "hi" + char(34) + ", שלום")
classes.example:
? o1.ToJSON()
#--> "say \"hi\", שלום"
? o1.ToCSV()
#--> "say ""hi"", שלום"
? o1.ToXML()
#--> say "hi", שלום
? o1.IsURL()
#--> 0

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds an input-output helper over a text or over a stzString object, to save it, load it or convert it to another format.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: a text, or a stzString object, to write out or to fill from a file

warnings: any other kind of value raises "Can't create stzStringIO! Parameter must be a string or stzString object."; Given a stzString object, FromFile and LoadFrom leave that stzString EMPTY while the helper holds the file content; the writing methods do not touch it. Pass the text, os.Content(), to be safe

methods.name: FileExists
methods.brief: TRUE if a file exists at the given path.

parameters.name: pcFilePath

notes: it tests a path, not the text held

methods.name: IsFilePath
methods.brief: TRUE if the text looks like a file path: it contains a slash or backslash and also a dot.
notes: it never looks at the disk
warnings: A shape test only: "http://x.org/a.b" and the number "1.5/2" answer TRUE, and a path without a dot, "dir/file", answers FALSE

methods.name: IsURL
methods.brief: TRUE if the text begins with http://, https:// or ftp://, in any case.
notes: "www.example.org" is FALSE: the scheme is required

methods.name: IsEmail
methods.brief: TRUE if the text contains both an @ and a dot, anywhere.
notes: the Hebrew "שלום@דוא.com" answers TRUE
warnings: A loose check: "@." and "x.y@z" answer TRUE, and "a@b" answers FALSE; it does not validate an address

methods.name: ToJSON
methods.brief: Returns the text as a JSON string literal: in double quotes, with quote, backslash, newline, return and tab escaped.
methods.returns: a text starting and ending with a double quote
notes: Hebrew, Arabic and emoji are kept as they are, not written as \u escapes

methods.name: ToCSV
methods.brief: Returns the text as one CSV field: in double quotes, with quotes doubled, when it holds a comma, a quote or a newline; unchanged otherwise.
notes: a comma, a quote or a newline triggers the quoting; plain text stays as it is

methods.name: ToXML
methods.brief: Returns the text with the five XML special characters replaced by their entities: & < > " and the apostrophe.
notes: it makes content safe to place inside an XML element, not a whole document

methods.name: ToHTML
methods.brief: Returns the text made safe for HTML and wrapped in a span element.

methods.name: FromClipboard
methods.brief: Raises the error "Clipboard access is not supported in this environment!" today.
notes: no clipboard is read
warnings: Always raises, it is a placeholder

methods.name: IsBase64
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is not empty and made only of letters, digits, +, / and =.
notes: it checks neither the length nor the padding
warnings: A character test only: "abc" and "====" answer TRUE although neither is valid base64, and a text with a space or a Hebrew letter answers FALSE

classes.name: stzStringLeadTrail
classes.brief: Looks at the two ends of a text: runs of repeated characters, prefixes and suffixes to test, strip or make sure of.
classes.description: It is the helper behind the ends-of-a-string methods of stzString (RemoveRepeatedLeadingCharsCS, EnsurePrefixCS, RemoveFromStartCS...), which builds one over itself and writes the result back; reach for it directly with new stzStringLeadTrail(cText) when you only need the ends. The reads (RepeatedLeadingChars, StartsWith, LeadingChar...) answer a text, a number or TRUE or FALSE; the verbs (RemoveFromStart, EnsurePrefix, RemoveThisLeadingChar...) change the held text in place and return nothing, the Q form returning the helper so calls chain; the past-tense forms (RemovedFromStart, PrefixEnsured) return the new text and leave the helper alone. Read the result with Content. A run needs at least two identical characters: a single leading character is not repeated. Matching is case-sensitive by default; StartsWithCS, EndsWithCS, EnsurePrefixCS and EnsureSuffixCS honour a case flag, while RepeatedLeadingCharsCS, RepeatedTrailingCharsCS (and so the Has and Number forms built on them) ignore it, and RemoveFromStartCS and RemoveFromEndCS do nothing for a flag of 0 when the case differs. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji runs are measured as you expect. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: an in-place edit through the helper empties the stzString that was passed in.
classes.example:
? o1.RepeatedLeadingChars()
#--> aaa
? o1.NumberOfRepeatedTrailingChars()
#--> 3
? o1.RepeatedLeadingCharsRemoved()
#--> abccc
o2 = new stzStringLeadTrail("example.com")
o2.EnsurePrefix("https://")
? o2.Content()
#--> https://example.com
o3 = new stzStringLeadTrail("םםםשלום!!")
? o3.NumberOfRepeatedLeadingChars()
#--> 3
o4 = new stzStringLeadTrail("😀😀😀ok😀😀")
? o4.RepeatedTrailingCharsRemoved() = "😀😀😀ok😀"
#--> 1

methods.name: init

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: the text to examine or edit, or a stzString whose content is used, any other value raises an error

notes: pass a plain text and read the result with Content; stzString does it safely by writing the helper result back with Update
warnings: with a stzString argument, the first in-place edit (RemoveRepeatedLeadingChars, RemoveFromStart, EnsurePrefix...) leaves the stzString you passed reading as an empty text, while the reads and the past-tense forms leave it alone; the helper itself keeps the right text

methods.returns: a text such as aaa; an empty text when the run is a single character
notes: the run is returned whole, aaabccc answers aaa
warnings: the RepeatedLeadingCharsCS form ignores its case flag: with the flag at 0, xXxy still answers an empty text, because the comparison is always case-sensitive

extensions.name: RepeatedLeadingCharsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

classes.name: stzStringLines
classes.brief: Works on a text line by line: counts, picks, sorts, reverses, deduplicates, indents and filters its lines.
classes.description: It is the line helper of stzString; build one with StzStringLinesQ (or new stzStringLines) over a multi-line text. Lines end at a line feed, and a final line feed makes one more, empty, last line. Each verb without an ending (SortLines, ReverseLinesOrder, IndentLines, RemoveDuplicateLines, RemoveEmptyLines) changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the helper so calls chain), and the matching form (EmptyLinesRemoved, LinesSorted, LinesOrderReversed, LinesIndented, DuplicateLinesRemoved) returns the new text and leaves the helper alone. Read the result with Content. Lengths count characters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji lines are measured as you read them. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: editing through the helper empties the stzString that was passed in. NumberOfEmptyLines does not count blank lines today (it subtracts a text length from a line count): count the empty texts in Lines instead. A carriage return before a line feed stays at the end of its line.
classes.example:
? o1.NumberOfLines()
#--> 3
? o1.LongestLine()
#--> apple
? @@( o1.NLastLines(2) )
#--> [ "fig", "apple" ]
o2 = StzStringLinesQ("שלום" + char(10) + "עולם יפה")
? o2.LongestLine()
#--> עולם יפה

classes.name: stzStringList
classes.brief: Holds a list of strings and answers questions about it: find, count, sort, filter, replace, split and change case.
classes.description: Reach for it when the strings of a list are the subject and a stzList is more than you need. It checks at birth that every item is a string, and the per-string work goes to the engine. Methods such as Add, SortInAscending, Unique, ToUpper and Trim change the list in place; the Sorted, Uppercased and Trimmed forms return a plain Ring list and leave it alone. Search methods come in a case-sensitive form and a CS form that takes a flag, as in FindCS(pcStr, 0).

classes.name: stzStringLocale
classes.brief: Answers questions about a text that depend on its script, its reading direction and its locale.
classes.description: It wraps a stzString and asks the engine, which counts Unicode characters and not bytes. Case conversion takes a locale, so Turkish dotted and dotless i come out right. Script tests tell the writing system, and a text that mixes two of them, the shape of a homograph attack, is reported by IsMixedScript; digits and spaces never count as a script of their own there. Known limit today: Hebrew letters are not seen as right to left (see DetectDirection), and LocaleCompare orders by character with case ignored, not by the rules of a language.
classes.example:
? o1.ScriptName()
#--> Latin
? o1.ContainsDigits()
#--> 1

classes.name: stzStringNumbers
classes.brief: Reads the numbers written inside a text, and sums, ranks, replaces or removes them.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringNumbers("text"); stzString does not hand one out. Numbers returns the figures in order as numbers: a sign directly before a digit belongs to the figure, a point between two digits makes a decimal, and only ASCII digits count, so Arabic-Indic digits and the 1 and 0 of 1,000 are read as the characters they are. The statistics (SumOfNumbers, MaxNumber, MinNumber, AverageOfNumbers, NthNumber) are built on Numbers; Max, Min, Average and the First, Last and Nth readers raise when the text holds no number, whereas the sum answers 0. RemoveNumbers and ReplaceNumbers edit the held text in place and work digit run by digit run, so the signs and points stay; NumbersRemoved and NumbersReplaced return the edited text and leave the object alone. Found today: a run with two points such as 1.2.3 raises R41 in Numbers and everything built on it; ScanInteger stops the Ring process above 2147483647; and the in-place edits on an object built from a stzString leave that stzString empty.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzStringNumbers("Invoice 12 costs -3.5 and +7, total 10")
classes.example:
? @@( o1.Numbers() )
#--> [ 12, -3.50, 7, 10 ]
? o1.SumOfNumbers()
#--> 25.50
? o1.NthNumber(2)
#--> -3.50
o2 = new stzStringNumbers("שלום 12 עולם 7.5")
? @@( o2.PositionsOfNumbers() )
#--> [ 6, 14, 16 ]
o3 = new stzStringNumbers("a😀1😀22")
? @@( o3.Numbers() )
#--> [ 1, 22 ]

classes.name: stzStringPerformer
classes.brief: Applies an expression to each character of a text and collects the results, as a list; the in-place Perform verbs do nothing today.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringPerformer("abc"). An expression is text in which @char is the current character and @i its position, such as "upper(@char)" or "@char + @char"; len() inside it counts bytes. Yield returns the result for every character as a list and YieldOn for chosen positions. Perform and PerformOn are meant to rewrite the text and leave it unchanged today, and the W forms (PerformW, YieldW) raise error R14. Use Yield and rebuild the text from the list when you need a rewritten string.

classes.name: stzStringRandomizer
classes.brief: Shuffles a text and draws from it at random: characters, words, sections, random case, random removal.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringRandomizer("text"). The drawing methods (RandomChar, RandomChars, NRandomChars, RandomSection, RandomWord) only read; the in-place verbs (Shuffle, ShuffleWords, RandomCase, RandomRemove) change the text held and have passive twins that return a changed copy (Shuffled, WordsShuffled, RandomCased). The randomness is the engine's random integer, so no two calls need agree; what stays fixed is what a result is made of, its length and its letters. Do not pass a stzString object you still need: the first in-place edit empties it. RandomInsert empties the text in most calls today.
classes.example:
? len(o1.Shuffled())
#--> 11
? lower(o1.RandomCased())
#--> hello world
? len(o1.RandomChars(4))
#--> 4
? len(o1.RandomSection(5))
#--> 5

classes.name: stzStringRemover
classes.brief: Deletes parts of a text: a substring, an occurrence, a position or section, the spaces, the repeats or what lies between two bounds.
classes.description: It is the removal helper behind many Remove methods of stzString, which builds one over itself and writes the result back; build one directly when you only need the removals. Each verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the remover so calls chain), and the form that ends in -Removed returns the new text and leaves the remover alone. Read the result with Content. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is cut where you expect. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: editing through a remover empties the stzString that was passed in. The case-flag forms (CS) of the first, last, nth, from-left, from-right and between removals ignore their flag today, and the nth rank starts at 0 here. An end position before a start position, or a closing-bound removal (IB) that finds no pair, kills the Ring process.
classes.example:
o1.RemoveFirst("an")
? o1.Content()
#--> bana split
o2 = new stzStringRemover("שלום עולם")
o2.RemoveSpaces()
? o2.Content()
#--> שלוםעולם
o3 = new stzStringRemover("a😀b😀c")
? o3.CharRemovedAt(2)
#--> ab😀c

classes.name: stzStringReplacer
classes.brief: Substitutes parts of a text: a substring, an occurrence, a position, the characters of a set, a pair of bounds or a regex match.
classes.description: It is the substitution helper behind many Replace methods of stzString, which builds one over itself and writes the result back; build one directly when you only need the replacements. Each verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the replacer so calls chain), and the form in the past tense (Replaced, Surrounded) returns the new text and leaves the replacer alone. Read the result with Content. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is cut where you expect, except in ReplaceByMany. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: apart from Replace, an edit through a replacer empties the stzString that was passed in. The ranks of ReplaceNth start at 1 but the default RemoveNth starts at 0, RemoveFirst removes the second occurrence and RemoveLast removes nothing, unless the case flag is given as 0.
classes.example:
o1.Replace("world", "all")
? o1.Content()
#--> hello all
o2 = new stzStringReplacer("שלום עולם")
o2.Surround("«", "»")
? o2.Content()
#--> «שלום עולם»
o3 = new stzStringReplacer("a😀b😀c")
? o3.Replaced("😀", "-")
#--> a-b-c

classes.name: stzStringSections
classes.brief: Cuts sections out of a text by position: reads a section or a range, lists what lies outside, and removes sections.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringSections("text"). A section is a pair of positions, start and end, both included; a range is a start and a length. Positions count from 1 in characters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji are cut by letter. The readers (Section, Range, Sections, AntiSections) raise for positions outside the text, while the removals clip them. The in-place removals have passive twins that return the text (SectionRemoved, SectionsRemoved, RangeRemoved). Do not pass a stzString object you still need: the first in-place removal empties it. A length of 0 and SectionBetween for close positions go wrong, and RemoveSections needs its pairs in ascending order; see the warnings.
classes.example:
? o1.Section(2, 4)
#--> bcd
? o1.Range(3, 3)
#--> cde
? @@( o1.AntiSections([ [ 3, 4 ] ]) )
#--> [ "ab", "efghij" ]
? o1.SectionRemoved(3, 5)
#--> abfghij

warnings: Given a stzString object, the first in-place removal (RemoveSection, RemoveSections, RemoveRange) leaves that stzString EMPTY while the reader holds the result; the readers and the passive forms do not. Pass the text, os.Content(), to be safe

classes.name: stzStringSplitter
classes.brief: Cuts a text into pieces at fragments, positions or regex matches, with or without keeping the separators.
classes.description: It is the splitting helper of stzString, which builds one over itself for its Split family; build one with new stzStringSplitter("text") when you only need to split. Split and SplitAt drop the separators, SplitBefore and SplitAfter keep them on the piece next to them, so joining the pieces gives the text back. A position names a character, not a byte, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is cut where you expect, and a position split drops the character at that position. The CS forms take 0 to ignore case. Found today: SplitAtSubStrings cuts at a literal <<<SEP>>> in the text, and a splitter built from a stzString object reads an empty text once that string is appended to.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.Split(",") )
#--> [ "a", "b", "", "c" ]
? @@( o1.SplitAfter(",") )
#--> [ "a,", "b,", ",", "c" ]
o2 = new stzStringSplitter("שלום עולם, שלום")
? @@( o2.Split(" ") )
#--> [ "שלום", "עולם,", "שלום" ]
o3 = new stzStringSplitter("a😀b😀c")
? @@( o3.SplitAtPosition(2) )
#--> [ "a", "b😀c" ]

classes.name: stzStringSubString
classes.brief: Studies one fragment inside a text with comparisons that always respect case.
classes.description: It is stzStringSubStringCS with the case flag fixed at 1, so it takes the fragment and the text and nothing else; every method is inherited and described on stzStringSubStringCS. Build one with StzStringSubStringQ(fragment, text).
classes.example:
? o1.NumberOfOccurrence()
#--> 4
? o1.LastPosition()
#--> 12

parameters.name: pcSubStr
parameters.role: the fragment to study

parameters.name: pcStr
parameters.role: the text it is looked for in, or a pair [ :in, text ]

notes: the same class as stzStringSubStringCS with the case flag fixed at 1; build one with StzStringSubStringQ(fragment, text)
warnings: a value that is not text raises Can't create stzStringSubStringCS

classes.name: stzStringSubStringCS
classes.brief: Studies one fragment inside a text: where it occurs, how often, what the text becomes without it, and how it sits among other fragments.
classes.description: Built with a fragment, a text and a flag that says whether comparisons respect case (1) or ignore it (0); stzStringSubString is the same class with the flag fixed at 1. Nothing here changes either text: the Replaced, Removed, Uppercased and Lowercased forms return a new text. Positions count characters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is located where you expect. Found today: Positions and Occurrences raise R14 because they call a finder method that does not exist; NumberOfOccurrence and Replaced do not count overlapping occurrences while Sections and NthPosition do; and IsBoundedBy compares the enclosed stretch with the fragment exactly, so the flag 0 does not reach that last step.
classes.example:
? o1.FirstPosition()
#--> 2
? @@( o1.Sections() )
#--> [ [ 2, 3 ], [ 4, 5 ], [ 9, 10 ], [ 12, 13 ] ]
? o1.Removed()
#--> Ba bda
o2 = new stzStringSubStringCS("AN", "Banana bandana", 0)
? o2.NumberOfOccurrence()
#--> 4
o3 = new stzStringSubStringCS("ל", "שלום עולם", 1)
? o3.LastPosition()
#--> 8
o4 = new stzStringSubStringCS("😀", "a😀b😀", 1)
? @@( o4.Sections() )
#--> [ [ 2, 2 ], [ 4, 4 ] ]

methods.brief: Returns how many times the fragment occurs in the text, never counting two occurrences that overlap.
methods.returns: a number; 0 when absent or when the fragment is empty

classes.name: stzStringText
classes.brief: Answers questions about a text as prose: its words, sentences, paragraphs and lines, its writing systems, and common clean-ups.
classes.description: stzString builds one of these to answer Script, Words and the other text-level questions; build one directly with a text, or use stzText, which inherits from it and adds meaning-level methods. Words, sentences and lines follow the Unicode rules, so Hebrew, Arabic, Chinese and emoji text is segmented where a reader would expect. Verbs such as ReverseWords and Simplify change the held text in place and return nothing (the Q form returns the object so calls chain), and the past- tense form (WordsReversed, Simplified) returns the new text and leaves the object alone. Pass a plain text, not a stzString: the first edit made through the object empties the stzString that was passed in. Known defects today: UniqueWords keeps the punctuation stuck to a word, so ContainsWord misses it; ReverseEachWord and EachWordReversed break any non-ASCII word; OnlyScript, OnlyArabic and OnlyLatin raise errors; ToSentenceCase capitalizes only the first letter.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzStringText("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")
classes.example:
? o1.NumberOfWords()
#--> 9
? o1.WordsReversed()
#--> dog lazy the over jumps fox brown quick the
o2 = new stzStringText("שלום עולם")
? o2.WordsReversed()
#--> עולם שלום
? o2.Script()
#--> hebrew
o3 = new stzStringText("Hello 😀 world مرحبا")
? o3.Script()
#--> hybrid
? o3.NumberOfWords()
#--> 3

methods.name: NumberOfDistinctScripts

parameters.name: _cScript_

methods.name: ContainsScript

parameters.name: _cScript_

methods.name: ContainsLatinScript

methods.name: IsArabicScript

methods.name: IsHanScript

methods.name: IsHybridScript

parameters.name: _n_

methods.returns: a text; an empty text when the rank is outside the text

methods.name: LastWord

classes.name: stzStringTrimmer
classes.brief: Trims a text: white space at its ends, or a chosen character repeated at its start, its end or both.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringTrimmer("  text  "). Trim, TrimLeft and TrimRight (and their aliases TrimStart and TrimEnd) strip white space; TrimChar, TrimCharFromStart and TrimCharFromEnd strip one given character, whole letters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji work. Each in-place verb changes the text held and has a passive twin that returns the trimmed text (Trimmed, TrimmedLeft, CharTrimmed ...). The Left and Right forms of TrimChar are meant to follow the writing direction and do not today. Do not pass a stzString object you still need: the first in-place trim empties it.
classes.example:
? o1.Trimmed()
#--> hello world
? o1.TrimmedLeft()
#--> hello world  
o2 = new stzStringTrimmer("--a-b--")
? o2.CharTrimmed("-")
#--> a-b
o3 = new stzStringTrimmer("😀😀שלום😀")
? o3.CharTrimmed("😀")
#--> שלום

classes.name: stzStringUnicodeList
classes.brief: Holds a list of Unicode code points and turns it into characters, text and per-script checks.
classes.description: Reach for it when you hold numbers such as 1513 and want the text, or hold a text's code points and want to ask whether they are all letters, digits, symbols or in one script. It is built with StzStringUnicodeListQ(aList); stzString does not hand one out. The list is validated at birth: every item must be a number from 0 to 1114111. The AllAre... checks build the text of the code points and ask the engine, so one check on a long list costs a string build; they answer FALSE for an empty list. Sorted, Unique and Reversed return new lists and never change the one held.
classes.example:
? o1.ToString()
#--> Hi
? @@( o1.UnicodesAndChars() )
#--> [ [ 72, "H" ], [ 105, "i" ] ]
o2 = StzStringUnicodeListQ([ 1513, 1500, 1493, 1501 ])
? o2.ToString()
#--> שלום
? o2.AllAreHebrew()
#--> 1
o3 = StzStringUnicodeListQ([ 128512, 97, 128512 ])
? @@( o3.Chars() )
#--> [ "😀", "a", "😀" ]

methods.brief: Builds a list of Unicode code points, checking that every item is a number from 0 to 1114111.

parameters.name: aList
parameters.role: the list of code point numbers

notes: the object keeps the list as given; stzString does not build one, so reach it with StzStringUnicodeListQ(aList) or new stzStringUnicodeList(aList)

notes: position 2 of the codes of Hello gives 101
warnings: a position below 1 or past the end raises the error Out of range!

methods.returns: a list of texts, one character each; empty for an empty list
notes: the Hebrew code points 1513 1500 give the letters shin and lamed one by one; an emoji stays one item

methods.returns: a text; empty for an empty list
notes: String is the same call; the Arabic code points 1605 1585 1581 1576 1575 give the word marhaba

methods.brief: Returns each code point paired with its character.
methods.returns: a list of [ code point, character ] pairs
notes: 72 pairs with H

methods.returns: a list of [ character, code point ] pairs
notes: H pairs with 72

parameters.role: the code point number to look for

methods.brief: TRUE if the characters of the code points are all letters, in any script.
methods.returns: TRUE or FALSE, as 1 or 0; FALSE for an empty list
notes: Hebrew and Arabic letters count; Hi! is FALSE because of the sign

methods.name: AllAreDigits
methods.brief: TRUE if the characters of the code points are all digits, in any script.
methods.returns: TRUE or FALSE, as 1 or 0; FALSE for an empty list
notes: the Arabic-Indic digits 1634 and 1635 count

methods.name: AllArePunctuation
methods.brief: TRUE if the characters of the code points are all punctuation marks.
methods.returns: TRUE or FALSE, as 1 or 0; FALSE for an empty list
notes: ! , . are punctuation while $ + < are symbols

methods.name: AllAreSymbols
methods.brief: TRUE if the characters of the code points are all symbols, such as signs, currency marks and emoji.
methods.returns: TRUE or FALSE, as 1 or 0; FALSE for an empty list
notes: the emoji 128512 and the euro sign 8364 are symbols

methods.name: AllAreMarks
methods.brief: TRUE if the characters of the code points are all combining marks.
methods.returns: TRUE or FALSE, as 1 or 0; FALSE for an empty list
notes: the accents 769 and 768 are marks

notes: 945 946 947 give alpha beta gamma and TRUE

notes: 1055 1088 1080 give three Cyrillic letters and TRUE

notes: the code points of shalom give TRUE; adding an Arabic letter gives FALSE

notes: the list held is not changed; 72 101 108 108 111 gives 72 101 108 111

classes.name: stzStringVisualizer
classes.brief: Makes a text visible: prints it, marks where a character or substring occurs, frames it in a box, or wraps matches in markers.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringVisualizer("text"); it only reads, so a stzString passed in is never changed. Show, ShowShort and ShowNL print; VizFindChar, VizFind, Boxed, BoxedRounded, Stringify and Highlight return a text; EachCharBoxed returns a list of small boxes. The boxes use plain ASCII characters (dots, dashes and bars), so they print on any console, unlike the Unicode frames of stzStringBoxed. Widths count characters, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji are measured by letter.
classes.example:
? o1.VizFind("an")
#--> "banana band"
#-->  -^^^^---^^-
? o1.Highlight("an", "*")
#--> b*an**an*a b*an*d
? o1.Stringify()
#--> "banana band"

CharsFromTo and CharsWithStep answer lists of characters; WalkAndYield runs a piece of code on each visited character. AddWalker keeps a named walker of numbers, whose steps are given as a list, and Walker gives back the numbers it visits. A step of 0 in CharsWithStep or WalkAndYield never ends, so never give one. Positions count from 1 in characters.

classes.name: stzStringWords
classes.brief: Treats a text as a list of words: lists, counts and ranks them, finds the longest, and replaces or removes a word.
classes.description: Build one with new stzStringWords("text"). Words, NumberOfWords, NthWord, NFirstWords, NLastWords and the length and frequency readers cut words by Unicode word rules, so punctuation is dropped, "well-known" is two words and an emoji is none; UniqueWords and WordAtPosition cut at spaces only and keep punctuation, so the two families can disagree on the same text. WordFrequencies and MostFrequentWord fold case. ReplaceWord and RemoveWord change the text held, but rebuild it from the words, which drops all punctuation and extra spaces: use stzString.ReplaceCS when the text must stay as it is. Do not pass a stzString object you still need.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzStringWords("The quick brown fox, the lazy dog. THE end")
classes.example:
? @@( o1.Words() )
#--> [ "The", "quick", "brown", "fox", "the", "lazy", "dog", "THE", "end" ]
? o1.NumberOfWords()
#--> 9
? @@( o1.WordFrequencies()[1] )
#--> [ "The", 3 ]
? o1.LongestWord()
#--> quick
? o1.ContainsWord("fox")
#--> 1

classes.brief: Reads the .stzstyl style format, the text that ExportToStyl writes, into a hash list of its name, theme, layout and sections.
classes.description: A style has a header line, theme and layout lines, and the sections colors, fonts, edges, nodes, focus and custom, each holding indented key: value lines. Every section is parsed into a list of [ key, value ] pairs. Only a single-digit value becomes a number.
classes.example:
? o1.Parse("theme: dark")[:theme]
#--> dark

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a parser for the .stzstyl style format, which holds no state.

methods.brief: Reads a .stzstyl file and parses its text; raises error R35 when the file cannot be opened.

notes: gives what Parse gives for the text of the file

parameters.name: pcContent

classes.name: stzSuperApp
classes.brief: Holds several apps as worlds of one governed constellation, with a shared Commons and cross-world calls that must be bonded and cleared.
classes.description: A world is any app object registered by name, or another constellation, so constellations nest. A call from one world to another goes through CallAcross, which allows it only when both worlds are active, a bond declares the action and the ambient governance clears the caller; Why gives the reason, and Crossings keeps a timed log of every decision. A world can be retired, revived and swapped for a new object without losing its bonds. The Commons holds identities, sessions and a key-value store in a database you open with OpenCommonsOn. CallAcross decides and records; it does not call into the target world. Everything was run offline, with an in-memory database.
classes.example:
o1.AddWorld("resto", new stzApp("resto"))
o1.AddWorld("supplier", new stzApp("supplier"))
o1.Bond("resto", "supplier", "order-produce")
o1.GovDeclareRisk("order-produce", 2)
o1.GovGrant("resto", "order-produce")
o1.GovSetAuthority("resto", :Delegated)
? o1.CallAcross("resto", "supplier", "order-produce")
#--> 1
? o1.CallAcross("resto", "supplier", "raid")
#--> 0
? o1.Why()
#--> no bond declares 'raid' from 'resto' to 'supplier'.

classes.name: stzSupposition
classes.brief: Records what is supposed about a name, as an overlay on the world that WhatIs reads and that can be forgotten or committed.
classes.description: A supposition is the sentence Suppose X is a fruit: SupposeQ(name) builds it, IsAQ records the assumption and AndQ lets the sentence go on. The world of entities is not changed; WhatIs answers with the supposed types while they are held, ForgetSuppositions discards them and CommitSuppositions makes each one known to the world.
classes.example:
o1.IsAQ(:Fruit).AndQ().IsAQ(:Company)
? @@( SuppositionsSoFar() )
#--> [ [ "tomato", "fruit" ], [ "tomato", "company" ] ]
? @@( WhatIs("tomato") )
#--> [ "fruit", "company" ]
ForgetSuppositions()
? @@( WhatIs("tomato") )
#--> [ ]

classes.name: stzSurfacePlot
classes.brief: Draws parts of a whole as a treemap whose cell areas are proportional to the values: as text, SVG or PNG.
classes.description: Despite its name it draws no function surface: it is a composition plot. The data is positive numbers, or label = number pairs, and the largest values get the largest cells. ToString draws box-drawing borders with a name centred in each cell; ToSVG and ToPNG draw coloured rectangles with the name and the share of the total, which :ShowValues = 0 removes. Setters answer the plot itself so calls can be chained, unlike the other plot classes. In the text picture a name wider than its cell is cut at both ends (Support reads upp.), values and percentages together run into each other, and in the pixel picture parts too small for a label get none; see the warnings. Gallery: doc/gallery/stzSurfacePlot/budget.png (five departments), seen right by stzlib-docs visual pass (a model reading the PNG), 2026-10-05, not a person; manyparts.png (twelve parts, seven with no label), seen uncertain by the same pass; terminal.txt is the text picture, read as text and judged wrong because a label is clipped.

classes.name: stzSystemActor
classes.brief: Stands for whoever acts on a system and carries the capability kinds that decide what it may commit.
classes.description: An actor holds a set of capability kinds from one lattice: effectful, sensing, compute and inference, the same lattice as stzSystemCapabilities and stzAgentGraph. Whether a plan may commit is decided against it, and the load-bearing rule is that a language-model actor holds only inference: it can propose, but Can(effectful) is FALSE so it can commit nothing that touches reality. Expression is free, admission is governed. The posture (trusted, external or sandboxed) is the second axis of the same gate.
classes.example:
? o1.Can("sensing")
#--> 1
? o1.IsEffectful()
#--> 0
o1.GrantKind("effectful")
? o1.IsEffectful()
#--> 1
? o1.Posture()
#--> trusted

classes.name: stzSystemCall
classes.brief: Runs an external program from a command line or from a program and a list of arguments, and keeps its output and exit code.
classes.description: Build the call, run it, then read Output, Error and ExitCode. The command is run by the engine with no console window. A list of arguments given with SetArgs reaches a program that is not a shell one by one, with no shell parsing them; a command line that starts with a shell word such as echo or holds a pipe is wrapped to run through the shell. ReturnType asks for the output as text, as lines or as a number. Set the program and arguments only from values you trust, since the call starts a real process.
classes.example:
o1.Run()
? o1.Succeeded()
#--> 1
? o1.OutputAsLines()[1]
#--> hello world
? o1.ExitCode()
#--> 0

classes.name: stzSystemCapabilities
classes.brief: Holds what a system can do, as names from a closed catalog, each mapped to one of four lattice kinds.
classes.description: The catalog has nine capabilities: filesystem, process, network, environment, dynamic_load and gpio are effectful, threads is compute, clock is sensing and inference is inference. The kinds are the same lattice an actor holds in stzSystemActor, so ForActorKinds answers which of the system's capabilities an actor may exercise. A name outside the catalog raises an error.
classes.example:
? o1.Can("clock")
#--> 1
? o1.KindOf("network")
#--> effectful
? @@( o1.Kinds() )
#--> [ "effectful", "sensing", "compute" ]
? @@( o1.ForActorKinds([ "sensing" ]) )
#--> [ "clock" ]

classes.name: stzSystemProfile
classes.brief: Describes one system as a bundle of facts: its operating system, runtime, resources and capabilities.
classes.description: A profile is a named scope the code is written against. A live one (stzDevSystem, stzCurrentSystem) is filled from the machine; a declared one, made with DeclareSystem, holds only the values it was given, so a profile for Android answers android on a Windows machine. The capabilities are drawn from a closed list, and Forbids, Requires and CompareTo set a target against this system. A profile is saved to and read from a .stzsystem text file.
classes.example:
o1.SetOSName("android")
? o1.SystemClass()
#--> mobile
o1.SetCapabilityList([ "filesystem", "network", "clock" ])
? o1.Can("network")
#--> 1
? @@( o1.CapabilityKinds() )
#--> [ "effectful", "sensing" ]

classes.name: stzSystemScope
classes.brief: Checks feature code written for a deployment target: forbidden operations raise, operations the live machine lacks are rehearsed.
classes.description: A scope is the context feature code is written in. Each capability-tagged operation (ReadPin, Spawn, Connect, UseOp and the others) is compared with the target profile and with the live machine: the target forbids it, so an error is raised during development; the machine can do it, so it is native; the machine cannot, so it is rehearsed and kept for the lowering bridge. Nothing is performed: the scope classifies and records, it never runs the operation.
classes.receiver: p = new stzPlatformProfile("sol") p.WithApp(:firmware, :ESP32) o1 = p.App(:firmware).System()
classes.example:
? o1.OSName()
#--> espidf
? o1.Can("gpio")
#--> 1
? o1.Forbids("process")
#--> 1
? o1.NumberOfChecked()
#--> 0

classes.name: stzTable
classes.brief: Holds a table of named columns and numbered rows, and answers questions about its cells, rows and columns.
classes.description: Reach for it when data has columns that deserve a name and rows that deserve a position. The content is stored column by column, as [ name, list of cells ] pairs, so a column is reached by its name (case does not matter) or by its position, and a row only by its position. A table is built from rows whose first line holds the column names, from rows alone (the columns are then called col1, col2 ...), from a hash list of name = cells pairs, or from a [ columns, rows ] size pair. Mutators change the table in place and return nothing; the CQ forms and the Sorted and Filled families give a result without touching it. The class inherits stzList, so a method not defined here falls through to the list. Many names are alternative spellings of one method, and a good share of the class is unfinished: about 200 methods raise an error or do nothing today, and each of them says so in its brief and its warning.
classes.example:
? @@( o1.ColumnsNames() )
#--> [ "id", "employee", "salary" ]
? o1.NumberOfRows()
#--> 3
? @@( o1.Row(2) )
#--> [ "002", "Henri", 10890.10 ]

classes.name: stzTablex
classes.brief: Tests whether a stzTable fits a pattern written in a small regex-like language, such as {cols(3) & unique(name)}.
classes.description: A pattern is text in braces made of terms: cols, rows, col, row, cell, colname, hascol, property, contains, sorted, unique, duplicates, grouped, filtered, aggregated, transposed, calculated, coltype, colpattern, sumcol, avgcol, mincol, maxcol, nulls, completeness, numeric, alphabetic and format, written like cols(3) or sumcol(sales:>50000). Terms are joined by & (all must hold), a vertical bar (one must hold) and -> (a sequence), @! negates a term, @cs: makes it case-sensitive, and results are cached per pattern and table content. cols and rows take a number or a comparison: > and < are strict, >= and <= are at-least and at-most. A name the table does not have is simply not satisfied, it does not raise.
classes.example:
? o1.Pattern()
#--> "{cols(3)}"

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a table pattern from text such as {cols(3) & unique(name)} and parses it into tokens; a non-text value raises an error.

parameters.name: pcPattern
parameters.role: the pattern text, with or without braces

notes: the braces are added when missing; a term written without parentheses, such as {cols}, parses into a token with no constraint

methods.name: NormalizePattern
methods.brief: Trims the pattern text and wraps it in braces when it has none.

parameters.name: _cPattern_
parameters.role: the pattern text, with or without braces

methods.name: ParsePattern
methods.brief: Splits a braced pattern at its top-level -> into parts and parses each part into a token.

parameters.name: _cPattern_
parameters.role: the pattern text, with its braces

methods.returns: a list of tokens, each a list of [ key, value ] pairs; one token per part, so {cols(2) -> rows(1)} gives two
notes: a part joined by & or a vertical bar is ONE token, a conjunction or an alternation, holding its conditions

methods.name: SplitByOperator
methods.brief: Returns the parts of a text split at an operator that stands outside brackets.

parameters.name: cStr
parameters.role: the text to split

parameters.name: cOperator
parameters.role: the operator, such as "->"

methods.returns: a list of trimmed texts; "a->b->(c->d)" gives a, b and (c->d)
notes: an operator inside parentheses or braces does not split

methods.name: ParseAlternation
methods.brief: Parses a part whose terms are joined by a vertical bar into an alternation token holding the alternatives.

parameters.name: _cTokenStr_
parameters.role: the text of the part, with or without outer parentheses

methods.returns: a token: [ type, alternation ], [ alternatives, a list of tokens ] and [ negated, 0 ]

methods.name: ParseConjunction
methods.brief: Parses a part whose terms are joined by & into a conjunction token holding the conditions.

parameters.name: _cTokenStr_
parameters.role: the text of the part, with or without outer parentheses

methods.returns: a token: [ type, conjunction ], [ conditions, a list of tokens ] and [ negated, 0 ]

methods.name: ParseSingleToken
methods.brief: Parses one term such as unique(name) or @cs:contains(Ali) into a token: its type, value, constraints and flags.

parameters.name: _cTokenStr_
parameters.role: the text of one term

methods.returns: a token as a list of [ key, value ] pairs; [ ] for empty text; an ERROR token for a term it does not know
notes: @! sets negated, @cs: sets casesensitive, the quantifiers + * ? and n-m fill min and max, and Match never reads min and max; a term with no parentheses, such as cols, gets no constraint

methods.name: RemovePrefix
methods.brief: Removes the first of the given prefixes that the text starts with and returns the rest; the text is unchanged when none fits.

parameters.name: cStr
parameters.role: the text to shorten

parameters.name: aPrefixes

parameters.name: cConstraintStr

parameters.name: _cType_

methods.returns: a list of constraints; [ ] for empty text, any other type, or a text it does not read, such as 2-5 for rows
notes: the greater and less forms are strict: cols(>4) is false for exactly 4 columns; the at-least and at-most forms are written >= and <=

parameters.name: oTable
